speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: MESSAGES OF GREETINGS AND GOOD WISHES ON THE OCCASION OF THE 80TH ANNIVERSARY OF CONFEDERATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, hon. members, I am sure, will be interested to know that, on this the 80th anniversary of confederation, many communications of greetings and congratulation have been coming to Canada from different parts of the world. Among the number are some that have been received by His Excellency the Governor General, some by myself as Prime Minister and others by the Secretary of State for External Affairs.
It will be of interest were I to mention some of the communications that have been thus far received. There are, I understand, others on the way, and probably there will be many more before the day is over.
Among those already received, there is a communication from Queen Wilhelmina of the Netherlands. Her Majesty has sent a message of best wishes for the well-being and prosperity of Canada.
His Majesty King Paul I of the Hellenes extends congratulations and best wishes in the name of the people of Greece. A message has also been received from the Prime Minister of Greece, M. Maximos, conveying warm wishes for the prosperity of Canada, and a similar communication from the Greek Ambassador resident in Ottawa.
Generalissimo Chiang Kai-shek of China extends best wishes for the welfare and happiness of the Canadian people.
The President of Argentina, General Peron, has expressed good wishes from the government and people of Argentina for the well-being and prosperity of Canada. Other messages have been received from the Argentine Foreign Minister and the Argentine Ambassador at Ottawa.
From Premier Ramadier of France there is a message expressing "most cordial wishes for the future of the great Canadian nation to which we are linked by so many' bonds of friendship".
There is also a message from M. Unden, Minister of Foreign Affairs of Sweden who expresses "best wishes for our friends the Canadian people". Mr. Jan Masarvk, Minister of Foreign Affairs of Czechoslovakia, sends good wishes, at the same time recalling wartime contributions "which are being continued and which can never be forgotten". There is also a message from the Minister of Czechoslovakia resident in Ottawa. In addition to greetings received from ambassadors and ministers already mentioned, messages of greeting have also been received from the following ambassadors and ministers resident in Ottawa: the Ambassador of France, the Ambassador of Brazil, the Ambassador of Chile, the Minister of Cuba, the Charge d'Affaires ad interim of the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics, and the Charge d'Affaires ad interim of Switzerland.
Had it not been that a week or two ago an arrangement was made in pursuance of an agreement to take every possible means to expedite the business of the session. I would have been tempted to introduce in the house this afternoon a resolution with respect to this 80th anniversary of confederation, to which all 'hon. members might have felt free to speak. But I have assumed that by proceeding with the business of the house as rapidly as possible, particularly considering the length of the programme still to be overtaken, we would be discharging our duties in a way more acceptable to those whom we represent. At the same time, I should like in a word to say what I think must be much in the thoughts of all hon. members today.
4SSS
Dominion Day

Had time permitted, we should have been, glad to review the eight decades which have passed since confederation and to have dwelt with pardonable pride upon the manner in which, from a few scattered communities, Canada has developed in that time not only into a great nation but as well into a world power. I believe.that at this time hon. members will have a feeling of great thankfulness that our country on this anniversary is perhaps more united and prosperous than it has been at any time in its history; that we have been spared the calamities and disasters which have overtaken so many of the nations of the world; and that our relations with other nations almost without exception could not be happier than they are. I recall that the last time this house was in session on July 1, which was five years ago, the world was in the midst of the great war, and at a very critical stage of the war. At that time it was by no means certain what the outcome might be. I am sure I speak for all hon. members when I voice a feeling of thankfulness for fihe part which Canada was privileged to take in helping to preserve the freedom of mankind in that great conflict. We look back with justifiable pride on the part which our defence forces were able to take, along with those of allied and associated forces; the contributions made by our army, our navy, our air force and the merchant marine; what was done in the way of assisting in supplies of munitions and food, in finance, in organization for all kinds of patriotic activities; the work of the women as well as of men and our young people in that terrible period. It is a source of tremendous pride to us all that today we can rejoice in having participated as we did and helped in the winning of victory. Nor do we forget that in our own generation a like service was rendered by Canada in another world war. There is an equal cause for rejoicing at the part which Canada has since been privileged to take in its postwar work, in helping to relieve the suffering of and to rehabilitate those nations which were so terribly devastated by war; in being able, as we have been, in her hour of great privation to assist Britain financially; and in being able to assist the starving peoples of Europe in the liberal manner in which we have.
I think what perhaps will be a source of increasing pride to the people of Canada, and in particular to their representatives here, is the extent to which Canada's voice and influence has come to be felt for good in the many relations of nations; particularly is this true of relations within the British commonwealth, where Canada's part in the development and

shaping of the commonwealth and its spirit has been what it has; and also the very important part which our country has taken in the work of the great new world organization, the united nations, in which humanity at the moment is placing so largely its hopes for the future. Indeed, as I have said, Canada's voice has come to be the voice of one of the great powers in the world; and wherever it has been expressed, it has been expressed for the good of other nations as well as our own. In our relations with our great neighbour the United States, we have together worked out methods of understanding and cooperation which are an example to nations everywhere.
In conclusion may I draw attention to the rather unique circumstance that while eighty years ago four provinces were uniting to form confederation and to fulfil the dream that some day there might be a vast power of the combined British communities in the northern half of this continent which would strike across space and) time and include all the territory between the waters of the Atlantic and those of the Pacific, today we not only have the nine provinces united as they have been over a number of years but we have in our city a delegation of distinguished gentlemen from the island, of Newfoundland, who are examining and exploring with officials of the government of Canada and its ministers, the possibility of arriving at an agreement which would be to the mutual advantage of Newfoundland and Canada and which might serve to bring that island also into confederation. These are only a few of the many things for which we, as Canadians, have reason today not only to be proud, but also to be profoundly thankful.
In conclusion, may I express the hope that Canada throughout the future may be true to her great past, to which I have made scarcely more than a passing reference, and that our country may go on from year to year, over the decades and over the centuries, ever using her influence in a wider way to promote the cause of w'orld order and to further peace and good will among men and nations on this earth.

maintopic: MESSAGES OF GREETINGS AND GOOD WISHES ON THE OCCASION OF THE 80TH ANNIVERSARY OF CONFEDERATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to follow the appropriate example of brevity which was set by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) in observing this important occasion in the life of our country. I wish to associate our party with the eloquent words of the Prime Minister, which I think reflect the views and aspirations not only of the people's representatives in this parliament but of the people of Canada in general. I suppose on the occasion of an

Dominion Day
anniversary such as this a nation, just like am individual, would feel like reviewing the past, taking inventory of the present and attempting to chart the course for the future in the light of past and present. As the Prime Minister has said, Canada has reached out in her international and domestic affairs to the point where she can rightly be called one of the great nations of the world. I think that we who feel that this country played her full part in the winning of victory, will wish also to say to the world that this country is prepared also to make her maximum contribution toward the cause of winning and keeping permanent the peace which followed that war.
As the Prime Minister so well stated, this country has laid firm and true foundations as far as our humanitarian policy in international affairs is concerned. We cannot have a permanent and lasting peace if we are prepared to pay only a cheap price for that peace. Whatever the price of a lasting peace may be, it will fall far short of and be of much less consequence than the terribly tragic cost of war. So whatever the cost of honourable and self-respecting peace may be, this country must be prepared to pay it. May I go farther and say that bound up with the cost of that peace must also go the realization that in assessing its true position this country will find it cannot, as an island of relative good times and prosperity, survive in a surging international sea of distress, poverty and suffering. Canada must bring itself to realize this, because after all, in that realization is involved also the cost of the peace that we are now trying to make just and permanent.
I fervently hope and pray that this eightieth milestone in Canadian history since confederation may see all the Canadian people moving forward, resolute and determined, marching shoulder to shoulder, regardless of any differences that may exist within the country, toward a greater Canada and a stronger and more powerful commonwealth of nations, in a world of permanent peace and prosperity in the days that lie ahead.

maintopic: MESSAGES OF GREETINGS AND GOOD WISHES ON THE OCCASION OF THE 80TH ANNIVERSARY OF CONFEDERATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to associate this group with the sentiments which have been expressed by the two preceding speakers. Eighty years ago life in this Canada of ours was a fairly simple affair. We were concerned with organizing and putting on a better basis the relations, as the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) mentioned, of the scattered communities of our half of the continent. In that we have succeeded perhaps beyond the hopes of those who were carrying on the work at that time. Today, while we may not have completely and satisfactorily resolved our own
difficulties, we are engaged with the other nations of the world in trying to settle the complex relationships of a very complex world. I think the people of Canada do feel pleased and proud because of the contribution we have been able to make in the past few years, and I believe we all hope we shall not only continue that work, but that we may be able to do better. To me the great thing in our life in Canada is that the people, through and by the institutions handed down to us by those who have gone before, are able to organize and settle their own affairs by mutual compromise and cooperation. We cannot expect people to travel together if differences separate them. I believe it is only when we can resolve those differences and have the same objectives that we can hope to travel along together; and as the years go by my hope is that we may do that in greater and greater measure.
Mr. SOLON E. LOW (Peace River): Mr. Speaker, I feel that I should say just a word in support of the high and nctble sentiments that have been expressed today by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and the other speakers. I am proud of Canada. I am proud of the accomplishments of our great country. I am proud that I was born in Canada. As I look back over my short life as it has been associated with the history of this country I take more and more pride in the fact that this is where my parents settled in order that I might be born a Canadian.
Most of the fine things have been said, I think, but let me just add one hope to the list of hopes for the future. I think I speak for my group when I say I want to see Canada take her full place and full responsibility in a world community of nations. We have much to contribute, not alone of material wealth. Canada is a wealthy country in all ways, but we have not enough, nor could we possibly produce enough, to relieve the world of its great needs at this time. One thing we can do, however, and I hope we shall do. By maintaining our faith in the fundamental truths we can assist in a regeneration of faith throughout the world, that faith which is lagging so greatly in many countries. Furthermore I believe it will be possible for us in Canada to help in a regeneration of the hopes of the various peoples of the world, without which they will not be able to do very much to help themselves. Therein I think lies the greatest possibility for Canada to make a real contribution in future.
I join with the others who have spoken in praying God that we shall be true to the trust that is ours, and that in future we shall continue to be true Canadians.
Dominion Day

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Bracken) asked if I would make a statement to the house today about remaining legislation, and as to whether any measures of which notice has not already been given will be introduced. I said at the time I thought everything had been included in what was set forth in the statement I made to the house several weeks ago. I wish to say now I find I am right in that particular.
There is on the Votes and Proceedings of today notice of a measure to be introduced by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) and to which I made reference before. I draw special attention to its appearance in today's Votes and Proceedings. The Minister of Finance intends to introduce another bill of some importance, but not for the purpose of proceeding with it at this session. Rather it will be introduced so that it may be considered by hon. members between now and the next session of parliament. The bill is An Act to Amend and Consolidate the Income War Tax Act. As I say, it is being introduced solely for the information of the house. As the bill is lengthy and intricate it was thought by the government it would not be wise to proceed with it at this session, but that it should be taken up in the next session.
I wish to make clear, as I did before, that there may be some bills arising from reports to the house by committees. It is not likely that there will be many, but there will be at least one or two.
It is not the intention of the government to proceed with the bill to amend the Royal Canadian Mounted Police Act, or with the

Old Age Pensions
resolution respecting the conservation of fisheries on the high seas, both of which were announced to the house on May 21.
Again, as a result of discussion on the estimates, it may well be that some subject will come Up which the house may decide should be dealt with in some way other than merely by discussion on the estimates. I have in mind for example the question of the controlling of traffic on parliament hill, which has been referred to at different times and which, to meet the situation, may necessitate some small amendment to an existing measure.
With the exception of that type of measure which would arise out of discussion, I cannot think of any others it is intended to introduce at this time. It would not do for me to say there will be nothing else; something might arise between now and the close of the session which is totally unforeseen at the present time. However I hope there will not be anything; and at this time I know of nothing likely to come up.

Mr. Chairman, the house will recall that in 1937 when the amendments to the Old Age Pensions Act respecting blind persons were first introduced by the government under the present Prime Minister the age of forty was set as the qualifying age in conformity with the expressed wishes of the organizations chiefly interested in work with
blind persons in this country. The managing director of the Canadian National Institute for the Blind, Colonel E. A. Baker, expressed himself on behalf of his organization to the effect that pensions for the blind should begin at the age of forty years. The effect of the 1937 amendments was to make it possible for the organizations working with the blind to concentrate on the training and rehabilitation of the group under forty years of age. The government now proposes, by an amendment, which I am going to ask my colleague the Minister of Veterans Affairs to move, that the eligible age for the blind be lowered from 40 to 21 years. I am sure that this is a step which will commend itself to hon. members who are aware of the plight in which blind persons find themselves, and of the many deserving blind people who will now be given new hope and encouragement by the assistance provided by this amendment. I would ask my colleague, the Minister of Veterans Affairs to move:
That in section 5, line 12, the words "forty years" be deleted and the words "twenty-one years" substituted therefor.

speechtext: I wish to make one brief comment on the bill as a whole. In this measure the government has resolutely turned its back on the sunrise and turned its face towards the sunset. The sunrise would have been so glorious. We are living in an age of plenty; we are living in a land of abundance. There is no excuse whatsoever for this bouse passing a bill which at the very best will keep all the elderly people of Canada in a condition of deprivation. Meanwhile I will say that what I am now saying is entirely in order, that the bill which provides only $30 a month for the elder citizens of Canada, in an age of abundance, in a country like Canada, is simply pathetically inadequate; and I protest against it with every fibre of my being.

subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to add my protest to that of the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore). The week before last I had the privilege of spending a few days at the convention of the National Health League of

Canada in Montreal. In that convention one of the doctors told us he had recently treated a case of scurvy. We thought that scurvy went out with the sailing vessels. We thought it was the result of not having fresh food. But scurvy in this case was the result of an old age pension which, after the rent has been paid, does not permit the pensioner to eat. The result of this bill is to widen slightly the income allowed to a pensioner; but it does nothing really to meet the needs of pensioners in the matter of finding a place to stay and putting food on their tables. I must add to the words of the hon. member for Lethbridge that it is a disgrace and a reproach to the Canadian people that old age pensioners should be gradually dying of malnutrition.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I just wish to say one word before this bill passes. It will not bring very much hope or encouragement to the old people of this country, so meagre is the amount of the increase. But I hope the old people of Canada will be encouraged and will find hope in the long battle which members of parliament on all sides have put up in connection with this measure. The dissatisfaction which has been expressed here augurs well for something better in the future. It means that members of this house are not satisfied, and I trust that the battle which has been waged will give hope to the old age pensioners, even though the $5 increase certainly will not do so.

subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have not taken up any time of the house on this bill, but I wish now to register my protest, along with that of the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) and the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mrs. Strum), against the inadequacy of this measure. This year our national income is almost $12 billion, made possible mainly as a result of our old age pensioners of today; yet we are offering them $30 a month. If the minister's baby were stripped of its fine clothing I think it would be a rather puny baby; in fact, it is a puny baby in the eyes of the people of Canada today. We have had many grand speeches in this house, paying glowing tributes to the people of Canada and to their productive capacity, but we are offering our old age pensioners and our blind pensioners $30 a month, as the best this country can afford. I say it is about time that sane people administered the affairs of this country, if we cannot do any better for our old age pensioners than we are doing at the present time. I must go further and say that if members in this corner of the house are not allowed a little more

Old Age Pensions
latitude, then the sooner we close up here and give the keys to somebody else whom we ace condemning in this house time after time, the better it will be for the Canadian people. Democracy is supposed to rule. Let us have democracy here instead of what we have been having during the past weeks and months.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to say one last word on this bill. So far I have not contributed anything to this debate. It started with a man known as Judas Iscariot; and I hate to think of the figure "30" being applied to the old age pensioners of this country. And that is "30" for this afternoon.

position. You do not do a man a favour bylending him money which he cannot repay. All the figures I can give I gave before. The number concurred in in the province of British Columbia is 236, to a total amount of $458,069.24. The number not concurred in is six, to the value of $12,833.33. That is as far as the Department of Veterans Affairs is concerned. It is not broken down into constituencies, because I was under the impression that the only way in which this act was not functioning almost to the complete satisfaction of the veteran was in respect to what we are now legislating on. Those were the only matters on which we were getting complaints, and we are bringing in this bill so that the act will function one hundred per cent to the satisfaction of the veteran. I understood that these amendments would be concurred in without a great deal of question. If that is not the wish of the committee, of course we are in the hands of the committee.
In regard to the number declined, the banks have advised the Department of Finance of the number who applied. Of course there are also many applications pending. The only figures we have are those where applications have been granted. In regard to those declined, it is hard to say when a loan is declined because a man may come in and discuss the matter with a bank and not proceed with an application after talking it all over. The act had been in operation for only two and a half months, on March 31 last when the report we have was made. We could easily give the numbers that have actually been granted, but it would be a mistake to suppose that all the remainder-* the difference between those where we had actually given our consent and those granted- are not going through. As has been pointed out, as of March 31 last the applications concurred in by the Minister of Veterans Affairs numbered 1.154 and actually 495 had been completed. The remaining 600 would be in process of going through, either getting the necessary legal documents completed or purchasing the machinery or something of that sort. Veterans Affairs
for by hon. members is simply unavailable, that is all. I think that will commend itself to the members of the committee.
We keep in close touch with the veterans through the various branches of our department, and any veteran who feels that he is not being treated right by the bank is perfectly free to make his complaint. Our departmental officials took the attitude that if we could get these amendments through it would meet practically all the complaints we were getting. Hon. members know that I took this up with veterans' representatives in the various parties in the house and asked them if we could get these amendments through to cure the situation without great difficulty. I was pleased with and want to express my appreciation of the cooperation of the veterans' representatives in endeavouring to get these amendments through.

I do not think the parliamentary assistant has yet answered the hon. member for Fraser Valley. I want to go back a little further. This legislation was announced last August, and I could not say just how many veterans asked me after August when the legislation would become operative. I know that a great many veterans in my riding wanted financial assistance to get established in business and some finally got it from private individuals, friends and others. I do not know why, if this legislation was to assist the veterans, it took from last August until last January to become operative.
Following up the question under discussion this afternoon, I know a little bit, as almost a permanent borrower from the banks, about how they report to their head offices and all the minor details within the community that they go into. Have the banks been asked to show in their quarterly statement the number of veterans who have actually come to the banks and discussed the question of a loan? I think the banks should give that information in their quarterly reports. I agree with the parliamentary assistant that a great many people may come in and talk over a loan and be talked out of it by the bank manager. That is perfectly true, but there is no reason why the bank manager should not report these discussions to the head office, and why head office should not include that information in their quarterly report to the department. I cannot agree with the hon. member for Winnipeg South that it would be detrimental to the whole set-up; far from it. It is simply a matter of business which the Department of Veterans Affairs should ask the Department of Finance to do for them. The banks are not taking much of a chance on these loans.
Most people who could take advantage of the act could obtain a loan on their own resources anyway. I am speaking after a lot of experience with veterans. Has the parliamentary assistant asked the Department of Finance to have this information made available by the banks, and if not, will he do so, in the interests of the veterans and the country as a whole? I am not advocating that foolish loans should be made to everybody, but parliament should be informed as to how successfully the act is working.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
subtopic: BUSINESS AND PROFESSIONAL LOANS-PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO PARTNERSHIPS
speechtext: I can assure the hon. member that our department, in this matter as in all others, intends to follow this up very closely to see that the intention of parliament is carried out. It was proclaimed only on January 15, and had been in force only two and a half months when the banks made their first quarterly report-the, only one we have-and so it is impossible to give any figures as to loans declined which really mean anything. I also want to say that it has been very much in the mind of the Veterans Affairs Department to make sure that the act was carrying out the purpose for which it was passed, and that is why this amendment is before the house. It was felt that this would cure almost all the complaints that we were getting, and so we said we will put ourselves in the hands of the house and open the act to make it do what we wanted it to do. I assure hon. members that our department is taking a real interest in this act, as in all other parts of veterans legislation, in order to carry it out to the best possible advantage of the veteran.

subtopic: BUSINESS AND PROFESSIONAL LOANS-PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO PARTNERSHIPS
speechtext: Some hon. gentlemen seem to think that as soon as you pass a bill someone can sit down over night with pencil and paper and scribble out some regulations and that is the end of it. But the amount of time involved in preparing the regulations, first of all in making arrangements with the bank and then getting the regulations ready and submitting them to justice and to veterans affairs, and then trying to get the whole thing worked out, is considerable.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: BUSINESS AND PROFESSIONAL LOANS-PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO PARTNERSHIPS
speechtext: There was not a day lost.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: BUSINESS AND PROFESSIONAL LOANS-PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO PARTNERSHIPS
speechtext:
There was no time lost. Hon. members will realize that when we left here at the end of August last year these men had been working day and night, many of them, and they had; only a few days left in which to get their summer holidays, to which they were entitled. Since the act was given assent to, I have been close enough to the whole question to know that no time has been lost by the officials. A great deal of correspondence had to be exchanged between the different branches, and I myself had questions put to me many times by people who wanted to know when we would get the act into operation. I sometimes thought there was delay, but I was on the job in November and well into December and I can assure the committee that there was no delay that could have been avoided in getting the whole thing started.
This legislation this year seeks to aid in every way possible both from the angle of the Department of Defence, from the angle of the Department of Veterans Affairs and from our own point of view, to make it a success, and it can be a success. But there will be a little time in getting it worked out. I would suggest to those who are interested in veterans affairs that they suggest to the veteran that if he is contemplating asking for a loam he use the form which is set out in the regulations here, andi on that form make his application to the bank. Then it can come back to the Department of Finance and we can check up. But we have no way of checking up on private conversations between veterans and bank managers. If the veterans use the form available to them there will be every chance.
We want to encourage these men. The statement has been made that the banks have

nothing to lose. The government guarantees twenty-five per cent of the first million and fifteen per cent of the other, so that the banks have a stake in it; and, regardless of what some people think of the banks, the banks are interested in the progress of the country. Every man who makes a success of his business is an advantage to the banks, and therefore the banks have everything to gain in encouraging these men, if you want to put it on the coldest possible basis. I insist that the banks are trying to do a good job and we shall get it worked out.

subtopic: BUSINESS AND PROFESSIONAL LOANS-PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO PARTNERSHIPS
speechtext: Who questioned the banks?

subtopic: BUSINESS AND PROFESSIONAL LOANS-PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO PARTNERSHIPS
speechtext: Nobody.

subtopic: BUSINESS AND PROFESSIONAL LOANS-PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO PARTNERSHIPS
speechtext: Why then insinuate?

subtopic: BUSINESS AND PROFESSIONAL LOANS-PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO PARTNERSHIPS
speechtext: There is a case which I should like to bring to the attention to the parliamentary assistant. It has been before the department previously, but perhaps now it may be covered by this amended legislation, and I want to have the view of those in charge as to whether or not it would be covered. This was a young veteran who, in August, 1946, noticing in the newspapers that this particular legislation was about to be proclaimed, or was to become law a little later on, believing he had some rights with respect to the purchasing of a business, did purchase that business, giving a mortgage in connection with it. It was a tearoom business, and he gave a mortgage for $2,000. From information I have, it was at the rate of something like eight per cent per annum. Then, feeling that the loan was only for a short time, he made application because he calculated that he would be able to avail himself at once of the loan provided under this legislation. He found then, however, that he was stuck with the loan, that this act could not cover what they chose to call past indebtedness, and the result is that he is now stuck with an eight per cent mortgage over his head. He is in a difficult position financially. I am wondering whether this legislation now covers such a case, which has aroused the interest of one of the major branches of the Canadian Legion and which may be typical of some other veterans who probably are in the same position. Perhaps the parliamentary assistant can enlighten me.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: BUSINESS AND PROFESSIONAL LOANS-PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO PARTNERSHIPS
speechtext: The second amendment is the one dealing with that and it takes care of that very thing. That man will be able to get his loan once this amendment is made, other things being equally satisfactory.

subtopic: BUSINESS AND PROFESSIONAL LOANS-PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO PARTNERSHIPS
speechtext:
May I make a statement in connection with what the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance

Veterans Affairs
said, and I speak for private members. Some of us private members have to borrow money occasionally from the banks, and the banks have been very good to me. The parliamentary assistant is most unfair in his reference, probably because he is in a more fortunate position than we are. As to the suggestion about criticizing the banks, no member who has spoken has passed any criticism upon them. Why should we? The banks cannot lose. The people of Canada are guaranteeing every dollar the banks are lending to the veteran; and it is most unfair for the parliamentary assistant, inadvertently I admit, to imply that when we, as private members, criticize this or any other bill, which is our right, we are criticizing the banks. There has been no criticism of the banks. I owe the banks some money today and I will borrow more tomorrow if they let me, and will enjoy doing so. It is unfair for him to say that we are criticizing the banks.

subtopic: BUSINESS AND PROFESSIONAL LOANS-PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO PARTNERSHIPS
speechtext:
I am pleased to see the government introducing this amending bill, no doubt after considering the suggestions made last year in the veterans committee. On a question like this we have to offer constructive criticism, and we must not be in too much of a hurry to criticize before the act has been in operation for a certain length of time. For once I cannot agree with the attitude of the hon. member for Fraser Valley. The hon. member for Winnipeg South made a sensible remark. This is a novel type of legislation, something entirely new in the field of loans, partly guaranteed by the government. I have no brief for the banks, but I have talked to a number of bank managers and I know the average bank manager will review any reasonable case and give the veteran all the breaks he can under the terms of the resolution. That is what I have found in my experience. As the hon. member for Winnipeg South said, we are doing no favour to a man by lending him money if he has not a reasonable chance of success.
I wish to make a suggestion with regard to the question of reporting the applications? I have talked to a number of men. You are bound to have large numbers of men without previous experience, possibly lacking in judgment in some instances, who think, because of this legislation, there is an opportunity to borrow some money, and become established in business where their future is assured. With these men going to the bank, explaining their circumstances, when the bank manager sees at once that the proposition they have to offer is unreasonable, is unlikely of success, he can tell them so. But if, after discussing the matter with the bank manager, the veteran wishes to make application, then he makes written application to the bank manager and I think those applications should be reported to the Department of Veterans Affairs. Of men who spoke to me and who were wishing to make applications to the bank for a loan under this act, I know of a few cases on which it would simply b,e a waste of the official's time, a waste of stationery and a waste of the time of everybody concerned to make complete reports, because the men either misunderstood the act or were endeavouring to go into some proposition which was thoroughly unsound in the first instance.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: BUSINESS AND PROFESSIONAL LOANS-PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO PARTNERSHIPS
speechtext: I probably gave a little bit of wrong information to the hon. member for Peel. You cannot borrow money from the bank to pay off old accounts. But where a man entered into an agreement between September 1 and January 15-that is, after the act had been passed, he went into it-he can pay that off with this loan. It could be used, in other words, as a part of the loan.

subtopic: BUSINESS AND PROFESSIONAL LOANS-PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO PARTNERSHIPS
speechtext: As his cash payment.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: BUSINESS AND PROFESSIONAL LOANS-PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO PARTNERSHIPS
speechtext: As his payment.

subtopic: BUSINESS AND PROFESSIONAL LOANS-PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO PARTNERSHIPS
speechtext: Is that not all?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: BUSINESS AND PROFESSIONAL LOANS-PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO PARTNERSHIPS
speechtext: That is all.

subtopic: BUSINESS AND PROFESSIONAL LOANS-PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO PARTNERSHIPS
speechtext:
May I get this thing
straight? The position is, I think, exactly as I indicated in my earlier remarks. It does look like a chance for this parliament at least to come to the rescue of someone such as the man to whom I referred. It really was not past indebtedness in the ordinary sense of the term, because it was indebtedness incurred with the belief that he could avail himself at once of the terms of this legislation when it was proclaimed. That is a little bit different from the case of a veteran who, without any thought or knowledge of an act of this kind coming into effect, perhaps incurred some indebtedness. This seems to be on a different basis from that, and I was hoping that the parliamentary assistant's first explanation would be the one that was tenable, because it would relieve a situation in a bona fide case, where the veteran is in a difficult position.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
subtopic: BUSINESS AND PROFESSIONAL LOANS-PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO PARTNERSHIPS
speechtext:
As hon. members will
recall, the committee gave a great deal of consideration to this question of whether money could be borrowed to pay off any existing indebtedness. After careful consideration, it was felt that it would be difficult to permit that in order to cover a legitimate case such as the hon. member for Peel has mentioned, but at the same time not open the door to having unloaded under this act loans which were made and were turning
Veterans Affairs

out or had turned out to be bad. It was finally the feeling of the committee that you could not permit a loan to be made under this act for the purpose of paying off any existing indebtedness, because it would be open to abuse. That is, a person might make a loan which looked to be good but which turned out to be bad. Then what could be better than to unload it under this act upon the dominion government? So the committee came to the conclusion that it would be unsafe to do that. Hence you cannot borrow money under this act except for the purposes set out in the act, which is to advance the veteran in the ways prescribed.	You
cannot borrow money under the act to pay off existing indebtedness, because it was feared that might lead to abuse. I may say that, as members of the committee will recall, we gave a great deal of consideration tc that feature.

subtopic: BUSINESS AND PROFESSIONAL LOANS-PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO PARTNERSHIPS
speechtext: Is no discretion possible?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
subtopic: BUSINESS AND PROFESSIONAL LOANS-PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO PARTNERSHIPS
speechtext:
Then there is danger of
abuse.

subtopic: BUSINESS AND PROFESSIONAL LOANS-PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO PARTNERSHIPS
speechtext:
My case is similar to that
mentioned by the hon. member for Peel. Last September three airmen entered into an agreement to construct a good-sized restaurant and dance hall in the suburbs of Halifax, and borrowed money when this act was being considered. The parliamentary assistant should look at it in the light of the fact that it was part of an undertaking entered into, as suggested by the hon. member for Peel. They entered into the transaction on the understanding that it would be brought within the scope of this act when it came into effect. For that reason I think the case referred to by the hon. member for Peel, as well as the one mentioned by me, should be considered in that light, and that favourable attention should be given to their request that a loan be approved to carry out the provisions of the building agreement.
I could go into a more extended review of this case, but I do not think it is necessary. The parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance has the file. I was hoping that the amendment proposed by this bill would be broad enough to take care of this particular case. Before a decision is given against the hon. member for Peel, I suggest to the parliamentary assistant that he give the matter further thought. I feel that the intention of the original act was to assist young servicemen to establish themselves in business by providing the necessary funds. Having that in mind, and also the fact that these men and no doubt others entered into agreements

such as I have mentioned, I hope the interpretation will be wide enough to meet the situation.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
subtopic: BUSINESS AND PROFESSIONAL LOANS-PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO PARTNERSHIPS
speechtext: Section 3 (1) (iv) of the act prescribes that a loan may be made to a veteran for "any purpose as prescribed which may be deemed to benefit his business." I suppose, if a person had taken on a load of debt at a high rate of interest, for the purpose of going into business, and that load was strangling his changes of success, and there was a chance of getting it at a low rate of interest and spreading it over a long period of time, that might be considered as a purpose "which may be deemed to benefit his business". I think it would be fair to say that will be taken into consideration as a suggestion, if there are many cases which seem to be legitimate, that consideration be given to the possibility of taking care of such cases under the section which I have cited. But, of course, it would have to .be circumscribed and laid down with a great deal of care so that it would not be subject to abuse.

subtopic: BUSINESS AND PROFESSIONAL LOANS-PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO PARTNERSHIPS
speechtext: I do not think there is very much in the argument which the parliamentary assistant has put up, that following the suggestion made by the hon. member for Peel in regard to people who have secured loans in order to buy businesses, in anticipation of getting a loan under this particular act, would lead to abuses and that a great number of bad loans would be unloaded on the government. I do not think there is any validity in that argument, for this reason: Every one of those loans must be approved by a bank manager. I do not think any bank manager who has been holding that job for any length of time in this country will recommend a second loan to pay off what has turned out to be a bad loan, because he would take into consideration there would not be a very good chance of the loan being repaid. The fact that a bank manager has to approve the loan before it is made completely throws out the argument put.up by the hon. member for Rosthern.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
subtopic: BUSINESS AND PROFESSIONAL LOANS-PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO PARTNERSHIPS
speechtext:
The hon. member has missed the point. The committee had in mind seeing to it that this guarantee of twenty-five per cent of the first million dollars was used to the benefit of veterans, and not to enable any financial institution or anyone else to unload on the government a loan that seemed to be going bad. Remember, there is a heavy guarantee by the government in connection with these loans, and if some financial institution found that a loan which looked very good last fall seemed to be

Veterans Affairs
going bad, because of something that had happened in the meantime, if the right were given under this act to switch a loan of that kind it would simply mean they could unload that debt on the dominion government. That is the point I was trying to make; I am not saying anyone would do so, but the committee suggested that was something which should be borne in mind. I say, if we are to make provision for the case mentioned by the hon. member for Peel we shall have to follow the suggestion of the committee very care-full}' and see to it that it is not subject to abuse in any way.

subtopic: BUSINESS AND PROFESSIONAL LOANS-PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO PARTNERSHIPS
speechtext: I think what has been suggested would require an amendment to the act, would it not?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
subtopic: BUSINESS AND PROFESSIONAL LOANS-PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO PARTNERSHIPS
speechtext: It could be done by regulation.

subtopic: BUSINESS AND PROFESSIONAL LOANS-PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO PARTNERSHIPS
speechtext: It would only require a change in the regulations?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
subtopic: BUSINESS AND PROFESSIONAL LOANS-PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO PARTNERSHIPS
speechtext: Yes; any purpose which has been prescribed, which may be deemed to benefit the veteran's business.

subtopic: BUSINESS AND PROFESSIONAL LOANS-PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO PARTNERSHIPS
speechtext: Some time ago I asked as to the number of applications made to the banks and the number accepted. The parliamentary assistant stated there was no record of those which had been rejected, and I think he made a very good suggestion when he said anyone dissatisfied with the decision of the bank had the right to fill out the application and file it, in which case it would be on record. The parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs said his department had received a certain number of complaints in regard to loans being refused.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: BUSINESS AND PROFESSIONAL LOANS-PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO PARTNERSHIPS
speechtext:
Mainly in regard to
delays.

subtopic: BUSINESS AND PROFESSIONAL LOANS-PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO PARTNERSHIPS
speechtext: I am going to ask him to give the committee the number of complaints that have been received up to date, or to the latest date available, and the number of those complaints that would be taken care of by the amendments now suggested. He told us a large number would be taken care of by these amendments, and if we had those figures we would get a better picture.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
subtopic: BUSINESS AND PROFESSIONAL LOANS-PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO PARTNERSHIPS
speechtext:
I am sorry I have not those figures. I took the advice of our officer in charge of the matter. I did not ask him to go back over the files to see the exact number of complaints, but he told me these amendments would take care of practically all of them. If the hon. member wants the exact
number of complaints and just what proportion would be looked after by these amendments it would require going back over the files for the last four or five months, and I do not know whether that would serve any useful purpose. If the hon. member wants the information I suppose we can get it for him, but I should hope that would not hold up this bill. The main objection to the bill that came to me was in connection with the delay in getting it actually into operation, and the delay in getting the regulations promulgated. Once that was done and the act came into active operation, I am bound to say it worked even better than I expected, and that the response was much greater than I expected.

subtopic: BUSINESS AND PROFESSIONAL LOANS-PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO PARTNERSHIPS
speechtext:
Will the minister and the two parliamentary assistants see bo it that from now on they get information from the banks as to the applications that are rejected? This controversy arose out of the question I asked last evening, which was as to how many applications have been rejected. It is obvious that the government has not that information; but under paragraph (m) of subsection (1) of section 7 of the act, which deals with the regulations, we find this power:
... to require reports to be made periodically to the minister by a bank in respect of guaranteed loans.
Will the government undertake to have the information available in future as to the number of applications that have been rejected? I really think we are entitled to that information.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: BUSINESS AND PROFESSIONAL LOANS-PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO PARTNERSHIPS
speechtext: I think the request is most reasonable. I believe a report should be made by the banks quarterly, or possibly more frequently, giving the information my hon. friend requests. I also want to tell him that if he looks at the correspondence he will see that the Department of Veterans Affairs was most persistent and aggressive in getting more immediate action in regard to this measure.

subtopic: BUSINESS AND PROFESSIONAL LOANS-PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO PARTNERSHIPS
speechtext: In other words, the Department of Finance were to blame?

subtopic: BUSINESS AND PROFESSIONAL LOANS-PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO PARTNERSHIPS
speechtext: I would not blame any department. The Department of Finance had some delicate negotiations to conduct with the banks. It was a new type of legislation, and difficult to put into operation. The Department of Finance have been most cooperative-

speechtext:
They were cooperative but a little slow; is that it?
490S
Veterans Affairs

subtopic: BUSINESS AND PROFESSIONAL LOANS-PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO PARTNERSHIPS
speechtext: Perhaps we were all a little slow; I do not know. Anyway, we were most persistent and aggressive, and I know the Department of Finance had difficult negotiations to conduct with ithe banks before they would agree to what we thought was a rational method of procedure in regard to these loans. That is the story.

subtopic: BUSINESS AND PROFESSIONAL LOANS-PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO PARTNERSHIPS
speechtext: I just want a little information, and then to offer a comment. I should like to ask the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs the grounds for non-concurrence in the twenty cases he mentioned a short time ago.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
subtopic: BUSINESS AND PROFESSIONAL LOANS-PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO PARTNERSHIPS
speechtext: The grounds were almost entirely that the persons were not veterans as defined in the act itself. The veteran must be a person resident and domiciled in Canada, who has received or is entitled to a gratuity under the War Service Grants Act, and who has not elected to take benefits under the Veterans' Land Act, 1942. Practically all cases of non-concurrence have been on one of those grounds.

subtopic: BUSINESS AND PROFESSIONAL LOANS-PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO PARTNERSHIPS
speechtext:
There would be practically no other ground on which the department could decide not to concur, because when the veterans affairs committee was sitting I believe it was established that only the banks had to right to refuse a loan, and all the Department of Veterans Affairs had to do was to identify the man to the bank as requested.
I should like to support the horn, member for Vancouver South and others who have asked for a report, not of every conversation a bank manager has with any fellow who might want to talk over a loan, but as regards those veterans who have actually made formal application and been formally refused. I think that is proper information.
One other matter was brought up here to which I think a little more careful study might be given. That was the question raised by the hon. member for Peel, in which we are all interested, the matter of making these loans in order to retire loans already made by other people. Take the case of a veteran who comes home and whose brother or some other relative lends him money to start up a business. Later the lender needs the money back. The veteran might try to arrange a loan under this act on a good, going concern, but the fact that he had a previous loan from somebody else would militate against his getting a loan from the bank. I believe the Department of Veterans Affairs should establish machinery of some bind to examine into cases of that sort and make it possible for veterans to get, under

this legislation, loans with which to repay loans previously obtained, so that they may continue with their business. In many cases those loans were made as a matter of family duty, out of pockets which were none too plentifully supplied with money.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
subtopic: BUSINESS AND PROFESSIONAL LOANS-PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO PARTNERSHIPS
speechtext: The matter will be studied, and if it is possible to do anything, it will be done.

Section agreed to.

subtopic: BUSINESS AND PROFESSIONAL LOANS-PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO PARTNERSHIPS
speechtext: I want to ask a question in regard to the date in this section, which I presume is the date this bill was given royal assent, in relation to people who embarked upon expenditures in order to secure a business, between that date and the time the act actually became operative.

subtopic: BUSINESS AND PROFESSIONAL LOANS-PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO PARTNERSHIPS
speechtext: That is the next section.

subtopic: BUSINESS AND PROFESSIONAL LOANS-PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO PARTNERSHIPS
speechtext: No, it is part of subsection (3) of section 2. I know of at least one or two cases where people did exactly what it is intended that this section shall cover, but they did it before royal assent was given. In other words, the measure was under consideration in the house. They were fairly sure it would become law, and they made expenditures in connection with the purchase of businesses, expecting that they could get loans afterwards. If they had done that between the first day of September of last year and January 15 of this year they would have been eligible under this amendment. However, they anticipated what might happen, and they are not eligible. I would ask that the date be moved back at least two months so that it would take in those who anticipated what was to take place.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: BUSINESS AND PROFESSIONAL LOANS-PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO PARTNERSHIPS

Why limit it to two months?
I was going to point out that some returned soldiers had entered into business before this act was in force. The intention is to give all returned men a chance to establish themselves in business. If one man was home sooner than the others, why should he be discriminated against? If it can be made retroactive for two months, why not six months? As has been suggested by the hon. member for Nanaimo, why not make it retroactive from the discharge of the soldier? I am sure the department will get into trouble if it makes it two months, because some will ask for three.

subtopic: BUSINESS AND PROFESSIONAL LOANS-PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO PARTNERSHIPS

Has any further consideration been given to making loans available where the veteran is going into a company rather than a partnership? That was the recommendation of the committee last year. That recommendation was not accepted by the government. The British Columbia command of the Canadian Legion passed a resolution in June of this year with regard to the Veterans Business and- Professional Loans Act, which states:
That loans be available for businesses which are incorporated provided that all stock in the organization is owned by the veterans engaged in the business, or their immediate families.

Section 3 agreed to.
On section 4-Bank security.

subtopic: BUSINESS AND PROFESSIONAL LOANS-PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO PARTNERSHIPS
speechtext:
The purpose of this amendment is to add the words "personal" and "or movable" in connection with collateral which a bank may accept as security when making a loan. It may be argued that a veteran is able to get a loan more readily if he is willing to put up all his personal property as collateral to satisfy the bank's requirements in respect of additional security. It would seem to me that this is a vicious principle and one in which we should not concur. The effect of it will be that a bank will tie everything up. It has been my experience that any time I go to a bank for a loan everything I possess is immediately tied up until the loan is satisfied. Where the furniture and personal chattells of a veteran are concerned, surely the government is not demanding the additional few ounces of flesh in addition to the pound it is already demanding by way of security.
Would one of the parliamentary assistants please justify this so that, with my limited intelligence of banking, I may understand it more clearly.

subtopic: BUSINESS AND PROFESSIONAL LOANS-PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO PARTNERSHIPS
speechtext: I am pleased with this amendment. There are several men in my constituency who purchased small sawmills in the last year. This amendment will permit them to offer as security that personal property.

The house resumed, from Monday, June 30, consideration in committee of Bill No. 362, respecting the protection and conservation of the forests on the eastern slope of the Rocky mountains-Mr. Mackenzie-Mr. Macdonald (Brantford City) in the chair.
On section 1-Short title.

subtopic: EASTERN SLOPE OF ROCKY MOUNTAINS- AGREEMENT WITH ALBERTA
speechtext:
The short title of this bill deals with the protection and conservation of forests on the eastern slope of the Rocky mountains. I would suggest that the dominion government has a strong, if not a direct interest. in the forest resources and that it should give real and continuing assistance to the efforts of all the provinces in the conservation of their forests. I suggest that, in so far as the eastern slope of the Rockies is concerned, the great hazard to the forests, namely, fire and the movement of insect pests, are not limited by

Forest Conservation
the actual topography of the ground or by provincial boundaries. Forest fires spread, quite heedless of whether the provincial boundary runs across the line of fire and insects spread quite irrespective of the height of ground or whether the forests are on the eastern or the westei-n slope of any particular range of mountains.
I have advocated in the last session that the federal government should show more interest in the development of our forest industries. I would point out that fifty per cent of the total lumber production for the whole of Canada comes from British Columbia and that of that fifty per cent, eighty per cent comes from what is known as the coastal region, where there is still much virgin timber. It seems to me that now is the time for the government to protect that virgin timber because, if that is not done, the time will come when the virgin timber has all been utilized, and we must ensure that by the time the virgin timber has been cut and turned into lumber there is a second crop coming up. It is only by ensuring that this second crop will be available at the time the virgin timber has been exhausted that we can assure that this country will be able to maintain its timber industry.
One-third of the territory of British Columbia is potentially productive either of agricultural products or of timber resources. But only one-sixth of that one-third is agricultural production, and the other ninety-four per cent is only productive if we can keep the timber growing.
The amount of export of timber from British Columbia is fifty per cent at least of the whole of the production of timber in the dominion, and the total export of timber is twenty-five per cent or one-quarter of the total exports of this country. The timber exports are second only to those of agriculture. Other governments, such as the governments of Australia, South Africa and the United Kingdom, have spent large amounts of money to ensure that the growing of timber is continued. and I suggest that Canada must stay in the timber business.
I should like to read into the record evidence which was given by Mr. H. R. MacMillan a short time ago when speaking before the commission of inquiry on forest resources of British Columbia:
The coast forest district (of British Columbia) produces over 80 per cent of the annual forest crop of this province. If the young coast forests do not burn, it appears certain that the coast forests will increase in absolute and in relative importance. The forests of the coast district produce more than 80 per cent of the public revenues from all forms of taxation based on forest income. The coast district also grows the largest crop annually per acre. The annual 83166-313J
growth per acre in the coast district is at least eight to ten times the average annual growth in the most productive forest regions east of the Cascade mountains. Growing as it does at an average distance of about twenty miles from the ocean and navigable waters, the coast forest, as compared with the interior forests, is more accessible to a larger provincial population and therefore more valuable as a support to large permanent communities and as a basis of a very important foreign trade. Therefore, it is reasonable to suggest that the immense forest resources of the coast forest district should be treated, not only as a separate administrative and protective unit, but also as a separate financial unit for protection purposes.
That last sentence refers to the action which is being taken by the provincial government. My whole point is this. I want to emphasize the paramount importance of concentrating efforts, not only on the eastern slopes of the Rockies, but also on the more valuable timber resources of British Columbia.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think it would be well at this stage if you would allow me to say something in a general way about the
Forest Conservation

the federal government for assistance. Ever since 1937, the matter of the protection of the forests, in the interests of the watershed of the east slope of the Rockies, has been under discussion between the federal government, particularly the Department of Mines and Resources, and the provincial department of lands and mines. From the beginning of this discussion the province has taken the stand that the protection of this east slope is of national importance and should, therefore, be financed largely by the federal government.
From the beginning of my experience in public affairs I can say that Alberta has been keenly interested in water conservation. She looked upon the protection of her watersheds1 as a sacred trust. Alberta has also been much interested in water utilization. I do not intend to deal with that; other speakers may wish to say something about it. But I contend that no other province in Canada has done so much in this regard. The interest of the people of my province in water utilization is undim-inshed; rather, I should say, it is growing yearly. Just as an indication of how important this is to the people of Alberta, and how we regard it, I should like to read one or two small extracts from a speech made by Hon. Mr. Manning, premier and provincial treasurer of Alberta, on the occasion of presenting his budget.

subtopic: EASTERN SLOPE OP ROCKY MOUNTAINS- AGREEMENT WITH ALBERTA
speechtext: This year?

subtopic: EASTERN SLOPE OP ROCKY MOUNTAINS- AGREEMENT WITH ALBERTA
speechtext:
Yes. By the way, this is his budget speech delivered on March 7, 1947. I find at page 6 the following statement by the premier:
In my address of last year, I mentioned the St. Mary's river development project as a part of a large scale irrigation programme which, when completed, would add some 345,000 acres of land in the Taber, Medicine Hat and Milk river areas to that already under irrigation. As a preliminary step, the province, the previous year, had undertaken the construction of the East Pothole Coulee dam. an integral part of the larger project. This work has been in progress for almost a year; and will be completed during the coming summer. During the past year, the dominion government awarded two contracts involving an expenditure of over $2,800.000; and construction is now well under way. Negotiations with the dominion government have been carried on for some time in an endeavour to work out a fair and equitable agreement whereby each government will carry its fair share of the cost of construction, colonizing and maintenance of the several proposed projects in the province. Substantial progress has been made along this line and I am hopeful that it will reach fruition in the very near future.
The project known as the Lethbridge southeastern or St. Mary's-Milk river will involve a total expenditure of a sum in excess of $15,000,000.
Just here, let me congratulate both the provincial government and the federal government when reaching that agreement and upon

getting on with the work of water utilization in the southern part of Alberta. Further to emphasize how this matter of water conservation and the protection of forests is regarded in that province I should like to read from page 16 of the same speech by Mr. Manning, where he says:
The estimates of the department of lands and mines are increased by $218,000.
That was over the estimates for the previous year.
A large portion of this is accounted for by two new appropriations-$30,000 to pay grants to municipal taxing authorities who are now restrained from levying mineral taxes-
But this one that follows is most important: -and $55,000 for the commencement of a forestry survey which will have great conserva-tional and commercial value. The balance of the increase in the department is mainly for the purpose of providing additional inspection and protection in our forest reserves.
To sum up what the minister said in this last extract from his budget speech, it simply means that a total of S190.000 over last year's votes for the department of lands and mines was to be spent this year for conservation and surveys on the east slope of the Rocky mountains. I believe there is much evidence that the province has realized fully the great importance of preserving the forests so that the run-off can be controlled and so that we shall have a constant supply of water in those rivers which rise in the east slope, not only for use in Alberta, but also in Saskatchewan and Manitoba, the provinces to the east. Alberta, but also in Saskatchewan and Manitoba, the provinces to the east. Alberta is still far out in the lead in the matter of conservation of the waters that fall upon this watershed. Alberta is also far out in the lead in the utilization of these waters, particularly in the areas of southern Alberta that were formerly considered drought areas. Alberta naturally would give every support to the bill now before us, and certainly I take pleasure in assuring the committee that this is a most worth-while measure.
In conclusion, may I emphasize one or two important matters that should be considered by the new board which is to be set up under this act. Hon. members will note that the bill provides that a board, to be known as the eastern Rockies forest conservation board, is to be set up, consisting of three members, two of whom shall be appointed by the federal government and one by the lieutenant governor in council, to take charge of the management, development, reclamation, reforestation and all those things concerned with the east slope of the Rockies. The bill also provides for a capital expenditure to be

Forest Conservation
borne by the federal government, covering a period of six years, of 86,300,000 for the location and construction of works for the purpose of making inventory of the forests, for the reforestation of the said area, and for other things that relate to the watershed.
When this board is finally set up and gets under way I hope it will recognize the great need for widespread education and instruction in individual responsibility on the part of the people in the area for the preservation of the watershed. Protection of the forests is not a matter that can be accomplished by a small board or by any particular group of men named by governments. Protection of the watersheds and forests of this whole country must be the individual responsibility of every citizen, not only those living in the area concerned, but also those living out on the plains, who may receive some benefit either directly or indirectly from that great heritage which is ours. That is why I appeal to the new board to take steps at the earliest possible moment to set up, in collaboration with the department of education of Alberta, high school courses, perhaps in composite high schools in the area, for the training of a forestry class of people. In most of the countries of the world where they have been successful in preserving their forests and keeping them free from predators, animal and human, and preserving the wild life, you will find that they have trained and established a forestry class of people. Sweden is a right good example of that, and Ontario has done something similar. I can think of no more useful thing for the board to do than to provide, not only training, but also work for the young people living in areas contiguous to the east slope of the Rockies, so that they can establish themselves and live useful lives in their own communities. Many times I have noticed the number of our young people who are forced by circumstances to go to far fields to seek their livelihood; and I think that is wrong. Here we have a chance to do something worth while to keep those young people in the area by training them in most useful and highly interesting work, that of reforestation, conservation, preservation, the study of wild life, and all that sort of thing. They would remain there, I am sure, for generations; they would be happy, and would feel they were contributing much to the wealth and welfare of this great country. Today we have even greater need of trained foresters than we have of trained agriculturists. I am not saying agriculture should take second place to forestry, but we already have a great number of trained agriculturists. So I say, without fear of contradiction, that
today we are in greater need of a trained forestry class than of further trained agriculturists.
I say this simply because authorities have agreed that we are wasting our resources much faster than it will be possible for us to reclaim them, unless we start right now on a conservation programme. Let me just read from an authority on this subject, by way of answer to anyone who may question what I have just said:
During the pioneer days of the dominion, and up to recent times, the immense natural wealth represented by Canada's forests had received little or no protection in the practice of conservation regarding its development. That is coming at last, but it has come too late to save the mighty firs and cedars of the Pacific coast. As one writer has already pointed out, we cannot wait for another thousand years to go by in order that we may increase our timber supply of this category.
Everywhere we must employ the strictest conservation of what is left, take only what is safe to take, and accept without criticism whatever quantity or quality may be officially allowed us.
Perhaps the board will have something to say about that sort of thing. Then he goes on;
*Reforestation-the planting of seedlings from forest nurseries-must be carried out on an ever-increasing scale, and only merchantable timber in properly regulated quantities must be taken. If we fail in this, history, in the near future, will indeed have a sad story to tell of the fate meted out to our vast forested regions.
Then he quotes some figures which I believe the committee should have before it to show the utter necessity of speed of action if we are to prevent disaster in Canada with respect to our forests. I shall quote some figures given by this man, Mr. J. L. Irwin, who for many years was an official in the department of lands and mines of Alberta. He says:
Statistical information covering Alberta's fire losses from October 1, 1930, to the close of the calendar year 1944 is given as follows.
And I would ask hon. members to note this particularly:

That is, the number of fires in all the forest reserves covering the greater part of the east slope was only 416. Then:
Number of fires outside forest reserves, 4,472.
These figures give some idea of the tremendous value of organization under forest reserves and under proper supervision by wardens and helpers.
Then:

That is tragic, in itself. As one travels through forests that are burned over and sees

I shall not trouble the committee with any more figures. I believe I have said sufficient to indicate how grateful for this bill are those of us who live in Alberta and who have come to realize the tremendous value of the forest, to Canada, not only from the point of view of merchantable timber, but more especially from that of the conservation of watersheds, to prevent floods in the spring and to make it possible to control the flow so that there will be a regular waiter supply the whole year, not only for Alberta, but for Saskatchewan and Manitoba.
I emphasize that we are keenly interested in doing our share. We are continuing to do it as a province, and I want the committee to know the provincial government is grateful to the dominion government for having brought forward this measure. We shall certainly give it our enthusiastic support.
Mr. MclvAY: Mr. Chairman, I wish to register my support of this measure. I support it particularly because I can see that in time it will confer certain benefits upon Saskatchewan and, indeed, upon the whole of Canada. I approach the subject somewhat differently from the honi. member for Peace River; but I believe he realizes, as do other hon. members, that we in Saskatchewan are very much concerned about the flow of water from the Rocky mountain slope.
We in Saskatchewan are irrigation conscious. As everyone should know, we are vitally concerned in this matter, because the flow of water we need for irrigation purposes must necessarily come from the area which has just been under discussion. The source of prairie water flow to which I have just referred, certainly in so far as the Saskatchewan river is con-

cerned, is in that mountain area, and is confined to the flow from the eastern slope of the Rocky mountains.
There the snowfall is heavy, and it is in the heavy snowfalls that the rivers -which flow through Saskatchewan and the plains to most parts of Manitoba and Alberta have their starting point. Any system of irrigation for the plains is inextricably linked up with the steady flow of water in those rivers. It is because of that I take this stand tonight in strongly supporting the eastern rocky mountain forest conservation bill now before the committee.
If the mountain and' foothills snows to which I have just referred melt too rapidly the waters rush away in flood, with the result that a large part of the water is lost. If the snow melts gradually, with the melting line going farther up the mountain sides as the summer advances, there will be a steady flow into the streams of the foothills, and thence into the prairie rivers such as the North and South Saskatchewan, which can be utilized in any irrigation project affecting the southern areas of Saskatchewan.
Many years ago in its primitive state the eastern slope was a densely forested area. When the slope was in that sthte it retarded the melting of the snows and provided a steady flow of water. But fire, the axe and the lack of a complete reforestation programme have denuded large sections of the slopes, with the result that the snows now melt rapidly and rush away in high tide, very often causing flood conditions.
In such a state these waters confer little benefit on either Alberta or Saskatchewan. The irrigation of the prairies is a highly desirable project and can be permanently effected only by reforesting, the eastern slope of the Rocky mountains, and by having the foothills reservoirs constructed so that the flow may be regulated. It seems to me that the protection of the source of the supply of water is the foundation upon which irrigation for the plains must be built, and the act of the government to ensure a continuity of water supply is one I highly commend.
Western people are now demanding irrigation projects, and a programme which is large enough to rehabilitate large sections of drought stricken areas. As I see it, this bill is a necessary step in that direction. May I express the hope now that irrigation will be one of the major post-war reconstruction projects for western Canada and that the west will not have to wait too long for its complete fulfilment.
