speechtext:
I rise not so much
to answer the questions because I have not the information, and I do not think anyone would have that information here at the moment-information at least of an estimated nature can be had and produced in due course-but to say that this bill provides for the maintenance of forests along the east side of the Rocky mountains and for other works which will make possible the conservation of water which has its source along the east side of the Rockies.
The bill provides for the expenditure of some S6,300,000 within a six-year period under a board of three. This is only one of three understandings that are being reached with the western provinces of Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba along the lines suggested by the last speaker. The first of the provisions is contained in this measure which provides for the conservation of water at its source and for the conservation of timber areas which make it possible to retain moisture over a greater length of time at its source rather than have it rush down to the sea in a short time without doing much good to anyone.
The rivers flow from this source through three prairie provinces to the Nelson river and the sea at Hudson bay. The three provinces are concerned with the water that has its source in the Rockies and, as a result there has been an arrangement agreed to by the province of Alberta. This is under discussion with the provinces of Saskatchewan and Manitoba. I speak of it now because this will probably be the only opportunity to report it to the house before carrying the discussions further with the provinces. I think it should be reported to the house before the discussions are carried further, and I hope they will be continued next week. It does not appear that there would be any opportunity until the supplementary estimates are down to report the matter to the house in any way excepting now.
I want to say now that, so far as the federal government is concerned, there is a provision for the setting up of a board of five to decide upon the distribution of water as it passes through these different streams, largely through the North and South Saskatchewan rivers, eventually into Saskatchewan, then
through Saskatchewan and into Manitoba. That board is to be composed of two members to be appointed by the federal government, one recommended by the Department of Mines and Resources and one by the P.F.R.A. organization under the Department of Agriculture, and a representative from each of the three provinces. The board will consist of officials who will receive no extra pay. They will be men who are engaged in this work and who will be called upon to meet from time to time to determine the proper division of water at the boundary lines of the different provinces, much in the way that the international water board determines the division of water at the international boundary line.
In addition to that, there is an arrangement being entered into based upon the principles contained in an agreement, which has been discussed, but is not in the form of a signed agreement as covering the project on the St. Mary's river. This resulted' from discussions with the Alberta government which were referred to a few moments ago by the hon. member for Peace River-relative to the St. Mary's dam. The understanding reached there is that the federal government will build the dam for the conservation of the water which will be utilized by organizations set up under the provincial irrigation act. The government has made provision for entering into agreements with the provinces of Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba by which the water will be conserved by the dominion and distributed by the provinces. There will be a point at which the full cost of distribution will be taken over by someone other than the dominion government. The dominion government would take certain action to conserve the water and some other organization set up locally would make use of the water.
In general terms those are the provisions that have been made by the three different arrangements. First, there is the provision to set up a board under this bill to conserve water at its source. Second, there is the provision to set up a board which will determine the division of water as among the provinces. Third, there is the provision for agreements with the provinces under which water will be utilized for irrigation and other purposes. I wanted to make this announcement in order that discussions with the provinces may go on more regularly and in order that the knowledge of those discussions might be placed before the house.

I would point out that during the last year a change has been made to which strong objection is taken by many members of the force. The period during which a police officer must serve before marriage was reduced to five years. In the period during which seven years' service was required one had to have only S500 available in cash to comply with the marriage regulations. That amount has been changed to SI,200 by an order issued on September 30, 1946, which provides that permission to marry will continue to be granted on completion of five years' service to those members who have proved their value to the force and in all respects meet with the regulations of paragraph 1313. That was changed in the fall of 1946 from S500 to S1.200. I would ask the minister whether consideration should not be given to restoring that to the former amount, representing the total assets of the police officer.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The reason that was changed was that too many men were running into debt. They were getting married on too small an amount.
You want to get the best possible men in the mounted police.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is right.

First, you make it difficult to get into the force, when it is considered that from January 1, 1946, 8,166 have applied to join the mounted police and, of those, only 566 have been accepted. The standard is so high that only exemplary persons can join the mounted police. Surely -we should not have a rule that weeds out the numbers who make application and then, after they get in, holds them to rules that I suggest are too strict and too stern. However, the minister has given the reason. But the mounted police managed to get along for many years under the rule of S500, and I personally know of only one man, in my many years of contact with the mounted police, wrho was ever seriously involved with overexpenditure in that connection. The minister has given the reason, but I ask consideration of the matter because these little

Supply-Royal Canadian Mounted Police
things cause a feeling of resentment that should not prevail in a force whose morale is always bound to be as high as that of the mounted police.
The second matter has to do with pensions, a matter that has been up before. It is the discrimination that apparently exists in the matter of pensions as between commissioned officers and non-commissioned officers. I will give an example. Section 52 of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police Act says, in effect, that upon the death of a commissioned officer his widow receives half his pension plus an allowance for each child. If the officer was not yet in receipt of a pension his widow receives an amount equal to one-half of the pension to which he would have been entitled if he had been, retired compulsorily immediately before his death. That applies to commissioned officers. But a non-commissioned officer who had served nineteen years in the force and died in service, not by reason of any act arising out of service, and who, if he had served one year more, would have been entitled to a pension left a widow who was denied any pension because that man was in the ranks. I give one example and ask the minister to give consideration to changing this provision. One particular police officer who would have had twenty years service in the spring of 1947 died in November, 1946. His widow is not eligible for one cent of pension. If he had lived a few months more he w'ould have been entitled, on retirement, to a pension of $67 a month. I suggest that some provision be made whereby the widow of the non-commissioned officer or man in those circumstances should be placed in the same position as the widow of a commissioned officer. It is a matter one often hears discussed. It is one that I am sure will appeal to the fairness and sense of justice of the minister.
The next matter has also to do with pensions, so that when the minister replies he can deal with pensions all at the one time if he will. Section 66 of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police Act reads as follows:
Any constable who has completed not less than twenty years service shall be entitled to retire and receive a pension for life.
One of the reasons why the minister says that the rate of wages is not as high as it might be, having regard to the responsibilities of the mounted police, is that there are attractive pension features. That was the argument advanced by the minister the other evening. My attention has been drawn to the case of a non-commissioned officer and the case of a constable who have served for more than twenty years and who, desiring to retire, are denied the right to do so. The non-83166-314i
commissioned officer applied for pension at the end of twenty-one years' service and was told he could have his discharge plus three weeks' annual leave, but he was refused pension when he made the request for retirement to which he was entitled. This particular case of the non-commissioned officer I bring to the minister's attention because there arc some 300 senior non-commissioned officers who have the right, to retire and are concerned about regulations such as that.
Before I go on to other matters, I will give the minister an opportunity to reply to the general question regarding pensions. It was raised in 1945 and the then minister of justice advised that the whole matter was being considered by an interdepartmental committee. I suggest, since the minister promised that consideration would be given, that the pension system should be arranged so as to make that which is applicable to the R.C.M.P. similar to that which is applicable to the permanent army, navy and air force.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The question of pensions for the Royal Canadian Mounted Police has received a great deal of consideration, and I hoped to be able to introduce amendments to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police Act this session, by which a different pension system would be put into force, but there have been so many difficulties in getting any agreement on that move that I am not able to introduce the legislation this session. The system is this. The officers have a contributory pension scheme. They make their contribution; the government makes its contribution, and then the officers and their dependents get certain pension benefits. But the men have a free scheme.
The officers plan only goes back to 1934.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I do not know what the history of it is, but that is the system at the present, time. Now, however, you have this peculiar fact in the R.C.M.P., that those other than officers have a free pension scheme. The men make no contribution at all, that is, so far as their own pensions are concerned. But they have themselves set up a pension scheme for their dependents to which the government makes no contribution whatsoever, and the regulation of that scheme is a matter for them. The government makes no contribution at all.
The hon. gentleman says that the scheme works out badly in some respects and perhaps it does. It may work out badly for the men and may work out badly in other ways as well, but up to date the representations I have
4920	COMMONS
Supply-Royal Canadian Mounted Police
received from the force are that they much prefer to retain their present two schemes, one for the men to which they do not contribute at all, and one for dependents, to which the government does not contribute, instead of having a new scheme which would be on all fours with that applicable to the military forces, which would be contributory entirely and which, in some respects, would be less beneficial to the men and, in other respects, more beneficial. It would be more like other pension schemes.
I have put a great deal of time, and so has the treasury, on the matter of pensions for the R.C.M.P., and it seems to be a problem which is more than ordinarily difficult as pension problems go. In any event, as the Prime Minister announced today, I shall not be ready with legislation this session. That is the first case the hon. gentleman mentioned. That is the case where a widow is not entitled to pension. That derives from a peculiar system applicable in the R.C.M.P., a system which, as I have said, has these two elements, a free pension plan so far as members of the force are concerned, a plan to which the men do not contribute at all, and a plan for their dependents to which the government does not contribute in any way. I intend to get the matter ready, and I have every expectation of getting it ready, for the next session. It is undoubtedly true that the pension provisions of the R.C.M.P. ought to be amended. They will not all be amended in favour of the men, because it is a generous scheme as the matter stands at the present time. Some of the amendments will probably make it better for the men but it will be a different plan in some respects from that which now exists.
The second point brought up by the hon. gentleman was the refusal by someone to allow a non-commissioned officer to retire at the end of twenty years. Certain wartime restrictions upon retirement were imposed-
This was in 1946.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am told that the restriction is now removed. They are going out much more freely than they were.

I am sure that the members of the force will welcome the statement made by the minister that consideration is being given to removing the unfairnesses and anomalies under which non-commissioned officers and men have suffered as a result of the pension law. In making these suggestions, I am trying to be as helpful as I can to see that these men receive the consideration to which they are entitled. The minister stated that there are difficulties. I know there are members of the bar in all parts of the house
rMr. Ilsley.]
who would willingly do their part to assist the minister in some committee that might be set up. I see across from me the hon. member for Spadina, who has devoted himself to this work and has a knowledge of it, and there are members on all sides of the house, who, I am sure, would give unstintingly of their services to produce an equitable pension situation so far as these men are concerned.
I pass now to one or two other matters. I refer to a question that arose last year out of the fact that certain non-commissioned officers and men resigned from the force, or rather at the termination of their period of service during the period of the war enlisted for overseas service. They served overseas for two or three years and, on their return, joined the mounted police once more. I raised the question on two or three occasions as to why these men, in the computation of their pension period, should not be entitled to count the time they served overseas, and also to their seniority being computed on the basis of their service in the force as well as the period during which they were in the armed forces overseas. The former minister of justice, acting on the advice of the senior officers of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, replied to me on two occasions. He informed me that the reason why that was not being done was that a circular had been sent out early in the war advising men in the mounted police that they were needed1 in Canada and indicating that if they joined the army they would forfeit their seniority. I have heard from members of the mounted police, both non-commissioned officers and men; and without exception they contend that there must be some mistake in that statement, because a search in the offices of at least a dozen detachments in this country does not reveal any such circular having been delivered. Whether it wa3 delivered or not-and I do not intend to enter into a controversy on that point-I contend that these men who served for years in the force and who, at the termination of their service felt that they could do more by serving overseas in the armed forces, should, not be punished for what I might call desertion for the purpose of active service. In other words, they should not be punished because in their desire to serve in the armed forces when their period in the mounted police was over, they chose to go overseas.
This situation has caused quite a bit of resentment among members of the force. They consider it is not fair to them that, having served, this should be denied to them. They also point out that they are denied credit for their period of service overseas in the compu-

Supply-Royal Canadian Mounted Police
tation of the period required' for qualification for stars. In other words, for every five years' service, whether in the armed forces or in the mounted police, a star is provided. These men who retired in this way and went overseas feel that they should not be denied the right to wear the stars of service because there was a break in the continuity of their service. Let me put it in this way. Suppose a man in the mounted police had served ten and a half years. His period of service was, say, ten years. His period of service was up. He went overseas. He comes back again and is reinstated. There are instances in which he is still being denied the right to wear his two stars which he had earned by service in the mounted police, because of the break in service occasioned by his enlistment. I ask the minister to remove these picayune things which cause a feeling that the service of these men is not appreciated.. These are the main representations I intend to make, and before I go ahead I shall give the minister an opportunity to answer.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not know very much about this armed service problem. Would the hon. gentleman make the same representations in favour of those who served in the armed sendees in Canada as for those who went overseas?
If they offered for active service.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: A great many of them did. A great many of them left the R.C.M.P. against the wishes of the R.C.M.P., on the promise of commissions and advancement in the armed services here in Canada, which they got. They even went back to the R.C.M.P. Some of them sought readmission, and some of them were readmitted. Just what particular obligations do the authorities of the R.C.M.P. owe these men in respect of promotion and advancement in this period I am talking about? Take the Canada ones to begin with.

If a man volunteered for the armed services, whether he served in Canada or overseas, he did so at the direction of the military authorities and he should not be penalized because his service was in one place or another.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
But the authorities of the nation requested1 these men to continue their service in the police force, just as they did with regard to the civil service in some respects. The rule was laid down in the civil service that civil servants, if they desired to enlist in the armed forces, should apply for leave; otherwise they would sever their connection with the service. It may be said that
when a nation is at war the authorities have no right to direct the services of their servants, the officials, or those who are discharging public duties. But I do not think a nation could be organized for war if that is not the case. Some weight should be given to the wishes of the police authorities at the outbreak of the war with regard to the service of these persons; because it must be borne in mind that there were many others who, in all probability, desired to retire and enlist, but who did not do so because they felt that they should not, having been requested not to. From experience, I know that was the case in the civil service. Men were told they should stay here and do their duty, for which they had peculiar qualifications. These civil servants saw others retire, go into the service, get commissions and much larger pay, and work just across the road from them here in Ottawa, in uniform. Later these men come back and want to get into the service again on the same terms as the others.	.

Would the minister permit a question? In 1939, No. 1 provost company was formed and went over with the first Canadian division. It was composed, I think I am correct in saying, entirely of members who had recently obtained their discharge from the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Oh, no-

They were employed
entirely on police duty.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.
In connection with the army.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Quite so.

Is it suggested that
the military authorities and the commissioner of the mounted police were not in agreement that these men should go?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Oh nio, I am glad the hon. gentleman mentioned that. We are not talking about those men at all. Those men did not sever their connection with the police force. Facilities were supplied by the police force for their service overseas in that organization. They went with the full blessing and consent of the police authorities, and they forfeit nothing; nor should they forfeit anything. It is the ones who did not pursue 'the course they were directed by their superiors to pursue, who severed their connection with the force contrary to the wishes of their superiors, who have forfeited these privileges.

I have heard so much about these directions being given by
4922	COMMONS
Supply-Royal Canadian Mounted Police
the superior officers. On two occasions the Minister of Justice has stated that a circular was issued and sent to the detachments. I have made the statement, on information received from over ten detachments, that a search fails to reveal that circular. I would ask the minister to clear up this matter by letting us see the circular and the date it was issued. He might lay it on the table, because these men say that such a circular was never drawn to their attention.

The minister asked the hon. member for Lake Centre whether he would differentiate between those who served in Canada and those who served overseas. May I ask the minister if the department is differentiating between an officer who left and went overseas, was wounded and decorated and then came back, and any other officer; whether he is treated a little differently from the man who sever got overseas. Is that the view of the department?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There is no differentiation.

We know that under the act passed last year the government demanded and insisted that men who left civilian employment to go into the army, no matter how much they might have been needed by their employers and no matter what important positions they might have held, be reemployed by the firms with which they had been employed at the time, and given the same status they had previously.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is right.
It seems to me that the government should be placed in the same position as civilian employers.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is just the point at issue, as to whether they should be on the same level or a different level, because the question enters as to the nation's authority in time of war, and whether the government should be on the same level as private firms.

The hon. member for Royal has brought to the attention of the house a situation that is anomalous, to say the least. Under the Reinstatement in Civil Employment Act, as he pointed out, every man who left a position and joined the armed forces is entitled to his job and his seniority. But if he were an employee of the government of Canada that situation does not prevail.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The hon. member is absolutely right.
I remember the former minister of justice saying that act does not apply to His Majesty the King.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Precisely.

Surely even at this date consideration should be given to assuring that what the king in the right of the Dominion of Canada asks of his subjects, he himself should be prepared to give to the employees of the dominion.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That sounds just beautiful, you know, but it is a generality that will not work out. The government has provided that men shall have certain rights to leave private employment, that employers shall have certain rights of discharge, and all that sort of thing, but certainly those same rules could not apply in the army. Yet if my hon. friend applied this resounding generality of his he would say that what the king requires or directs in regard to industry, and so on, shall apply in the government service. That is not necessarily so at all.

As far as the
mounted police were concerned they signed on for a definite period.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.

When that period ended, their contract with His Majesty ended. They determined then upon a course they were to follow. They said, "We are not going to sign on for a further period of three years; we are going to join the armed forces for active service." Surely the analogy the minister endeavours to draw does not apply to the position ' of affairs I have brought to his attention.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Do I understand that my hon. friend is talking about policemen whose contract with His Majesty was fully discharged and terminated?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
And who left at the end of
the contract?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If that happened in private industry there would be no obligation upon the employer to take the man back.

I am taking that
as an example.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Then why mention this civil reemployment act?

Evidently I have touched a sore point with the minister. All these men ask is that the facts be told. First, the government took the stand that the reason nothing could be done for these men, the reason they were being penalized for having gone overseas in many cases, was that a

Supply-Royal Canadian Mounted Police
circular had been issued. If that circular was issued, at least the minister would have found ground upon which to stand. That has been the answer for two years now, that such a circular was issued and that, in the face of the circular, these men who were serving in the mounted police joined the armed forces. They say no such circular was ever delivered to them. We can close off this discussion very quickly if the minister will table the circular in the house, advising the members of the force that they were needed in the mounted police in Canada and that if they joined the armed forces they would lose their rights. If such a circular were delivered I would withdraw my objection, because that has been the excuse always given me and the other hon. members who have raised this point. The government said, "Well, these men knew what they were doing. They followed a certain course". Every one of these men who has communicated with me says that he never knew of such a circular, and that a search of their detachment offices reveals no such circular. So I ask the minister this very simple question. Will he table the circular and let the committee know the date it was issued?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The commissioner advises me that this was a letter from the minister to the commissioner, published in general orders. I will table that.

The other evening I did not have a chance to follow the hon. member for Lake Centre when he discussed the regulations governing the members of the mounted police with respect to marriage. I was not greatly impressed with the minister's remarks on this subject. I think people who attach importance to the institution of marriage would agree that most people do more effective work after they are married than before, and I believe this would go for the personnel of the R.C.M.P. If it is difficult to get married men to serve with the R.C.M.P. in the north countrj' I suggest that the way to solve the problem is to make life in the north more attractive. During the war I remember travelling north to Churchill and meeting a member of the R.C.M.P. who was returning to one of the far northern posts. His wife had been born in the New England states. She was very happy to be getting back to the north after a boring holiday down in the area where she spent the first years of her life. On the same train were a number of Americans employed in construction work in the north. The lowest paid man in the party was to receive for a year $450 a month, with free transportation from his home in the United States to the north and everything found. Others were to receive $500 and $550
a month. In passing, 1 might mention that, since then, Canada has taken over the military installations constructed by these personnel. Naturally the member of the R.C.M.P. felt that his compensation appeared pretty small compared with the wages being paid those Americans who were going north. I think we should not have any regulations-

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext:
Where were those
Americans working?
In the far north.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: Whereabouts?

In the Hudson bay
area, one of the establishments about 500 miles north of Churchill.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext:
Where my hon. friend
comes from.

I never received quite so much for living in the north country. But we should not have any regulation saying that members of the staff should wait for five years, three years or two years before marrying. If they are accepted into the force it should be established that anywhere the union jack flies citizens of this country should be permitted to many.
I believe that in the past the Minister of Justice may have had some trouble in obtaining adequate budgets to meet the requirements of this work. But the minister had so much experience as Minister of Finance that I believe he will agree there should not be any insurmountable barrier in getting an adequate budget so that all the people who work under his administration may have an annual income adequate to support a family, if necessary. I do not think we should take the position that police officers who go up to Baffin Land, Coronation Gulf or Aklavik should be singled out as being barred from marriage.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: Or from Regina.

Anywhere in Canada.
I believe a member of the staff should be permitted to marry.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Hear, hear.

I should like to see
the minister agree with his genial colleague the Minister of Veterans Affairs who, I am pleased to say, supports me in my argument. I believe this whole question should be considered. We should not have regulations which interfere with the personal liberties of the subject.

Is the war duties pay taken into consideration in arriving at a pension? If so, on what basis, and as of what date?

Supply-Royal Canadian Mounted Police

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Yes, it is. It is regarded
as part of the pay. Then the hon. member asks as of what date. The pay was consolidated in October, 1946; and, for pension purposes, a member of the force is regarded as having received the consolidated pay even for the prior period back to 1942. But if he were pensioned prior to October 1, 1946, and pensioned on a lower basis, the pay not then having been consolidated, his higher pension dates only from October, 1946.
Is that quite fair?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I believe it is.

I have been told by men
who have retired from the force that if they retired before October 1, 1946, their war duties pay was not taken into consideration, although they 'had been drawing war duties pay for several years before retiring.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It is taken into account
for the pension they received from October, 1946, on, because October, 1946, was when it was consolidated.

But in respect of a man
who retired on September 1, 1946, is the war duties pay taken into consideration?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes. His September instalment of his pension, if there were such a thing, would be on the lower basis. But everything from October 1, on, would be on the higher basis.

A man retires a month
before the consolidation of the war duties pay and the ordinary pay. Is his pension based on his pay plus war duties pay?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: He gets his pension on the basis of pay including war duties pay from October 1, 1946. I am trying to say something accurate, although it is intricate.
It sounds intricate to me. Could the minister explain it a little more fully?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Does the hon. member understand what I am trying to say?
No, I do not, unfortunately.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Then I shall try to say it again. His pension from October 1, 1946, on, is based upon the higher rate of pay, regardless of when he retired.
I see.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: But the pension he received prior to October 1, 1946, is on the lower rate of pay.
Thank you.

As we know, many soldiers married overseas. Most of the wives have come out to Canada with the soldiers, but many of them have remained in England. Soldiers deserted their wives or, for some reason or another the wives did not get to Canada. I understand that the English law now provides for divorce for any woman in England who has been deserted by a Canadian, an American, an Australian or the member of any other force. My point is that we have many of these young returned soldiers in Canada whose wives are divorced from them in England. I understand that the English law does not apply in Canada, and that these men are left in a position where they cannot marry again. Then there are the soldiers whose wives will not come out to Canada. I know of a young man in my home town who came back to Canada, bought a site and built a house, but his wife would not come to this country.
This matter may not sound important. I know that we in Canada are averse to weakening our divorce laws. But this is a matter which the Canadian Legion is now considering, and it is being considered by other organizations throughout the country. There are many hundreds of these men. Has the minister's department given consideration to this matter? Has it been taken up with the provinces? I know our divorce laws and regulations are very indefinite on the point, and perhaps nothing could be done unless there had been consultation with the provinces. The matter is not as simple as some of my hon. friends may think. It is a serious matter for these young men who are compelled to live in this country a life of single blessedness, like the Minister of Veterans Affairs.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Leave me out of this.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I submit that the question is not even remotely related to the item.
I was out of the house when the department was called.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: We are discussing the general administration of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.
I thought it was the general item of the Department of Justice. If the minister does not care to answer at this time, I shall be content.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think I had better not.

Supply-Royal Canadian Mounted Police

This item deals with general police work. A reading of the commissioner's report would indicate that, even since the war, espionage is an everpresent factor and that our vigilance in this particular respect cannot be allowed to relax. He points out the necessity for keeping constant watch, and in support of that cites the espionage inquiry. We have not heard much about the activities of the mounted police in connection with that inquiry. Would the minister be prepared to advise the committee as to whether a section of the mounted police is devoted to looking into espionage activities? Within the last few days one of the outstanding newsmen in this dominion wrote an article which appeared in the Montreal Herald of Friday, June 27. This reads:
Hitherto untold secrets of the great spy roundup now reveal that the police wanted to arrest hundreds, not just the two dozen they finally tossed into barracks.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: Who is that written by?

Harold Dingman in Ottawa.
But today it can be revealed that the R.C.M.P. pleaded with the Minister of Justice- and the cabinet'-to let them jail up to 300 people suspected of being active red agents.
To what degree is that statement correct? Are any of those who were in the list of suspects still subject to investigation?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Neither of the two statements read by the hon. gentleman is true in any degree whatsoever.
The minister says there is no foundation?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No foundation for the statement and I do not know how it came to be written.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Demobilization and reconversion-
580. To provide for increased activities of the force, $1,864,142.

There is a reduction in the main Royal Canadian Mounted Police estimate, and yet here we have an item providing for increased activities of the force. What other services are to be rendered? What is the nature of the increased activities to which reference is made in this item?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
During the latter years of the war the estimates of the R.C.M.P. were carried under two headings, the ordinary estimates and the war appropriation estimates. In the fall of 1945, the war appropriation estimates were carried into the

The rules of the Supreme Court of Canada require that all appeals made to 'that court be printed. The cost of printing is heavy. In many cases it amounts to a denial of the right of appeal to a poor man. With the different methods we have of duplicating copies today, I think this rule should be changed. The Supreme Court of Canada no doubt makes its own rules; but, after all, we pay the money for administration, and I am satisfied that if the minister would bring this matter to the attention of the court something would be done to remedy what I consider a great injustice. In my own experience my client has been prevented from making an appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada by the heavy cost of printing. It varies with each case. I want to join with members of the bar everywhere in this country who commend the minister since he has become Minister of Justice for having appointed to the Supreme Court of Canada a judge of a different political persuasion from that of the government in power. It was a novel departure from the ordinary practice and one which, if followed, would, I think, lead to a great improvement in the judiciary of this country. In the United States the government in power endeavours to choose so far as possible the best men available. While some interpret the best man as meaning the best man within one's own party, the attitude taken in Washington is that at least one-quarter of the appointments could be made from outside the political party in power without impairing the efficiency of the judiciary.
I should now like to ask a number of questions in regard to the judges. Is it intended to continue the practice that became somewhat widespread during the war whereby certain judges, while remaining judges, took up positions in the public service of the country? I realize that during war time that could be understood. I wish to ask this question specifically. Some months ago the appointment was made to the ambassadorship in China of a judge of the court of appeal of Saskatchewan, the Hon. Mr. Justice T. C. Davis. He has not sat on the court of appeal since his appointment in 1939, which could be understood during the war, and recently he has been appointed to an ambassadorship. I would ask the minister whether or not Mr. Justice Davis has resigned as a judge, having been appointed to the diplomatic service.
I would also ask the minister what is being done with regard to the retirement of some of the elderly judges in our country. True, there are exceptions. Mr. Justice Avery in Great Britain has often been pointed out as an exception to the rule, but from time to time ministers of justice have endeavoured to arrive at some plan whereby retirement could be arranged for all judges over seventy-five years of age. The general scheme in that connection is to provide that at that age the pension shall equal the salary as judge, thereby removing any inducement on the part of the incumbent to remain in his position.
How many judges are there in the superior courts of the country over seventy-five years
of age? We had the figure last year, and I believe they have been increased during the last year.
The third question has to do with the exchequer court. From time to time complaints are received) that in this court there is not that celerity, if I may use the expression, in handing down judgments which should characterize the administration of justice. My information is that a considerable number of judgments are two and one-half years overdue. It is one thing to administer justice; it is another thing to administer delay. After all, one of the most important things in the administration of justice is that justice be done and not unnecessarily delayed. I would ask the minister how many judgments are overdue two and one-half years and how many are overdue two years, and what is being done to have these judgments handed down.
I have in mind one particular case, where the judge waited for a couple of years. He was not a judge who took many notes. He forgot the facts. He did not have a list of witnesses, but in time he handed down the judgment and it was a case of deciding whether he would dismiss the action or give judgment for the plaintiff. That is not justice, and that is one of the great dangers about indefinite postponements in handing down judgments. The facts are forgotten and, the facts being forgotten, the judgment may not be in accordance with the facts.
What is being done toward filling vacancies in the district courts of Saskatchewan? speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If I remember the questions asked by the hon. gentleman, I shall answer them briefly. The first question was as to the policy of the government in availing itself of the service of judges for positions in the public service. It is not the policy to do that save in exceptional circumstances, and it has been done to a very limited degree. There has been no resignation from Mr. Justice Davis.
Has he tendered his resignation conditionally?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I have no knowledge of any such thing and I feel sure I would have it. I can learn of nothing, conditional or otherwise.

The minister's
deputy would know.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There has been no resignation, conditional or otherwise. Of course it would be impossible to get the number of judges over seventy-five until tomorrow. If I had had notice of the question I could have had the information tonight, but it would take some little time to find out how many there are. I do not know whether the information is of sufficient importance to the hon. gentleman and the committee to justify delay.
I am wondering what is being done in order to secure retirement by the indirect route I suggest.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The method suggested by the hon. gentleman was pretty objectionable, I thought, and that was to make the pension equal to the salary. I do not like the sound of that or the content of it either. I do not think people should be paid just as high a pension as their salary. That might get them to leave and it might not.
You can not do it statutorily.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No. The British North America Act precludes us from doing it, and I have no particular plans for making any change in the situation. I think that the principle of the Supreme Court Act is a better one. I suppose there must have been some reason at some time for giving these judges this life tenure or tenure during good behavior. I suppose it was considered a protection of the independence of the judiciary. It seems to me, however, that it would be desirable if we could enact legislation by which they could retire at, seventy-five. We cannot do so, and I do not know that there is anything much we can do about the matter. If we field out a big financial bait to retire, the question is whether the remedy would not be worse than the wrong.

The minister has rather misinterpreted what I suggested. In 1933, as I remember, a measure was introduced in this house and passed, which provided that at seventy-five years of age the salary of the judge would be reduced to the amount that his pension would have been had he retired. That passed through the House of Commons and was turned down in the other place. I am not suggesting at all the payment of a pension equal to the salary, because in that case there might be some appointed at seventy-four who would then retire at seventy-five, which procedure certainly would be subject to objections.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I was not acquainted with that plan. It is ingenious, but it does not sound constitutional to me. I mean, if you can reduce salaries in order to force judges to retire, you can interfere pretty effectively with the rule that they hold office during good behaviour, which is guaranteed under the British North America Act.
I think the law officers of the then minister of justice advised that it was constitutional.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not know. I will look that up. It does not sound so to me.

The problems outlined by the hon. member for Lake Centre are important. Has the department given consideration to reducing the salaries by 81,000 a year, for instance, after judges pass the age of seventy? That would be constitutional, and it might result in getting around the difficulty.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not think the hon. member is serious about that. Under the British North America Act, judges hold office during good behaviour, which is for life.
We fix the salaries, though.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: But you could fix the salaries in such a way as to nullify the constitutional provision, I should think.
I would not think so; not after they have passed the age of seventy.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I do not think the salaries
can be juggled in such a way as to run the judges out in that way any more than they can be dismissed.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is right.

I intended to ask a
question in that regard, because I know of one case which has been before the exchequer court now for thirty-seven months. I shall give the minister the particulars of the case, but first I wish to ask him how cases are dealt with in the exchequer court. Are they dealt with in the order of priority in which they come before the court? If not, are priorities arrived at, and who decides which case shall be heard first if they are not heard in the order in which they come before the court ?
In the case of the property of persons of Japanese origin who were evaouated from the Pacific coast in 1942, there were three petitions of right instituted in the exchequer court in July, 1943. Permission to proceed was not obtained from the government until the following October, and a defence was not filed by the government until the following February. Therefore, as will be seen, these cases have really been in the courts for four years. Arrangements were then made to have the cases argued on the points of law involved, and this argument was heard at Ottawa by Hon. Mr. Justice Thorson, president of the exchequer court, on May 29 and 30, 1944, w'hen decision was reserved. I have a letter from the solicitors for the applicants, as I imagine they would be called in this case, which is March 1946. They say, "It is therefore almost two years that we have been waiting for a decision." I am wondering why a decision has not been given in those cases.
During the last few years I have heard a great deal in this house about the glories of the rule of law. If our law does not provide justice to our citizens without regard to their nationality or origin, I insist that it is not law; at least it is not law as I understand the use of the term. What I wish to know is whether there are cases which came before the exchequer court since these cases came before it, and in which judgments have been rendered. I should like to have some information on this matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The cases are not necessarily decided in the order in which they are begun; ttiat is, a case may be initiated in 1944, and no decision given until 1946, while in the meantime cases which were initiated in 1945 may result in decisions in 1945. I do not know that much more can be said about the matter than that. Much would depend upon the difficulty of the case, its importance and how long it took to deal with it. Of course something would depend upon the judge; there is no doubt about that. Some
judges are slower than others. Perhaps some judges take more pains than others. At any rate, some judges have a reputation for being more prompt with their decisions than others. The number of cases in arrears before the Exchequer Court of Canada has been made the subject of questions in the house this session, and returns have been tabled showing the number outstanding. My recollection is that some cases tried in 1944 have not yet been concluded. I should not like to say any more than that I regret that condition of affairs. But just what to do about it I do not know.

That, I submit, is a most unsatisfactory answer. Last year in this house we increased the salaries of judges and their pensions when they no longer earned salaries, or at least when they no longer drew salaries. Now we find that the administration of justice, and whether justice is to be delayed-and justice delayed is justice denied-depends wholly on the judge, and that nothing can be done about the matter. If a case comes before the courts, the judge can decide to lay it by, not to do anything about it, but to go on and deal with other cases. Surely that is not justice. It may be law', but it is certainly not justice.
I insist that here are people who appealed to the Canadian courts. They engaged respectable solicitors who conducted their appeal in the ordinary manner. Now, three years and one month after that case came before the court, it is still there, undecided. These people do not know where they stand. I just tell the minister that if the answer he gave me tonight is the only one he can give, there is certainly something wrong with our administration of justice.

I feel very much like the hon. member for Vancouver East. I have a great respect for the judiciary, and I sympathize with the feeling I assume the minister has, because it is a delicate matter, perhaps something which is not done at all, for the representative of justice, as the minister is, to say anything by way of urging these men to do what I would regard in plain words as their duty. It seems to me fantastic that this situation should exist. But if nothing else can be done it seems to me that there is certainly one thing the minister can do; that is, recognize this situation and draft other judges, if that can be done. I do not suppose there is any magic about the exchequer court, and other judges could be appointed to see that this situation is not perpetuated. I feel earnestly the truth of what has been said by the hon. member for Vancouver East, that this will bring the law
Supply-Justice

into disrepute and even into contempt, because I believe what my hon. friend has said about justice delayed being justice denied.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I want to point out that in recent years two additional judges have been added to the Exchequer Court of Canada.
Within what period?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Within two or three years.

Then I think it would be relevant to ask whether there is much sign that the situation is improving since the addition of those judges and, if not, whether others should be added. At any rate, I feel like my hon. friend to the left, that for the minister to say he does not know what can be done about the matter certainly to me is unsatisfactory.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The minister may have been a little indiscreet in saying that; but, in addition to the two additional judges who have been appointed, at various times three ad hoc judges have been appointed to help the work of the exchequer court. Still the fact remains that some cases are delayed for long periods. I do not know; there may be special reasons in the cases the hon. gentleman has mentioned, but I do know quite a number of cases are in arrears on the parit of one or two of the judges of the exchequer court. That was what I meant by saying I just do not know what to do about the matter.

Then I ask this further question with some hesitation and perhaps I should almost say with some deference, because I am not very familiar with the procedure in matters of this kind; but would it be going too far to say there should be almost a practice followed that, if judgments fall in arrears beyond a certain point, further judges should be appointed'? From the point of view of a layman, a sort of reformed lawyer like myself, the present situation does seem fantastic.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is not always the remedy. There have been and probably are instances in Canada where judgments have been in arrears for several years, and where it is well known that the court is large enough, so that the mere appointment of more judges would not be the remedy at all.

In some cases the reason for delay is the temperament of the judge, who wants to arrive at the truth and probably finds it difficult to make up his mind. That has occurred in every court in every province of this country. In Ontario many years ago

they amended the judicature act to provide that if a reserved judgment were not given within six months either party could apply for a new trial. Perhaps such a provision should be included in this act. I suppose it would require an amendment to the Exchequer Court Act, and perhaps the same thing should be done to the Supreme Court Act, but of course the difficulty with the exchequer court is that a single judge hears the case. I think such an amendment ought to be brought in by the minister. It would be helpful to the judge concerned if he knew he had to render judgment within a certain period. I remember a judge of the supreme court in Ontario who saw both sides of a case so clearly that he experienced great difficulty in coming to a decision. That judge was later appointed to the court of appeal, w'here he was a very fine and efficient judge.

The minister said a
moment ago there might be special circumstances in the case referred to by the hon. member for Vancouver East. I want to say that I do not think any .special circumstances can justify the withholding of a judgment in thp exchequer court or any other court for a period of three years. The case referred to by the hon. member is not unusual; others of us have had cases standing there for long periods of time. I am now awaiting judgment in a case where I appeared as counsel over two and a half years ago. A situation like this is a reproach to the Canadian judicial system. The minister says it may be attributable to the fact that there are not enough judges. Well, I do not know, but the fact of the matter is that the addiion of two judges to that court in recent years does not appear to have appreciably reduced the backlog of cases. But if that backlog is not attributable to the dearth of judges in that court, then I think the minister himself must admit some responsibility for keeping in touch with the situation there and urging upon the judges that some strong effort be made to reduce that backlog, particularly the cases that have been standing longest.
It cannot be viewed with anything short of great regret, to put it mildly, that litigants should be compelled to wait for such long periods of time. The rights of people are hanging in the balance. They go to the court to have those rights settled, and then those rights are left in suspense for these long periods. It cannot be said that our courts are offering justice when they hold cases for so long.
Probably the exchequer court is the most glaring example we have in Canada today in

Supply-Justice
this regard, but it is not the only court in which a situation of this kind has arisen. My colleague from High Park referred to the situation that existed in connection with one supreme court judge in Ontario. I recall a county court judge who became notorious for letting his judgments stand. He died some years ago with one case still undecided in which I had been awaiting judgment for no less than five years. I submit that situations of that kind cannot be permitted to continue. I appreciate the delicacy of the position in which the executive branch of the government finds itself in a situation of this kind; but it is so important that justice should be prompt, so important that there should not be these long delays in determining the rights of litigants who have gone to the court for a decision on their rights, that I submit the minister should approach a situation of this kind and deal with it. If there are not enough judges to cope with this big backlog, to reduce it and take care of the current cases within a reasonable time of their hearing, then I think the minister will have to address himself to that problem. Whatever the reason, whether it be shortage of judges or something else, I suggest that the remedy lies in the hands of the minister. If there is another reason I urge that the minister assume some responsibility, because I submit that the public is entitled to look to the Department of Justice for help.

Thank you. If I can do so without too much interruption it will not take long. I should like to ask the minister if ten people who have been acquitted of any guilt in connection with espionage trials will be reimbursed for their legal expenses. speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am at a loss to understand why a line should be drawn between certain persons who are acquitted and the great body of persons who are acquitted in criminal trials.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: No, none at all.

That answer does not mean anything. I know there are difficulties when there are different claimants, each of whom believes he is entitled to the appointment. speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Have there been any complaints to the government with regard to newsprint, and have any inquiries been made as to possible infractions of the Combines Investigation Act in that field? speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I received a long letter-[DOT]

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Would that be from Mr. Percy Bengough, president of the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think that is the one, and I think it is the only one if I remember correctly, although I may have received telegrams from some organizations, which I took to be labour organizations, suggesting that there was some combine in the manufacture of newsprint which was contrary to the Combines Investigation Act. speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Can the minister say where we go from here? This matter has been raised in the house on previous occasions and it seems to be a serious one. I noticed my hon. friend the hon. member for Vancouver South a few moments ago reading a copy of a paper from his city, the Vancouver Sun, which, I understand, has considerable difficulty in getting sufficient quantities of newsprint to meet its demands. I am also led to believe that a newspaper in Winnipeg which is seeking to get organized and get started has had considerable difficulty in getting any intimation that it can secure newsprint, although it is one of the products that is in pretty high production in Canada at the present time. My own inquiries resulted in my getting hold of certain documents put out by the newsprint people themselves, which indicated that, following the ending of control by the wartime prices and trade board, the newsprint people instituted their own control of the supply of that product. That control, in turn, seems to have these strange effects upon Canadian newspapers seeking newsprint. I know that involved in it is the whole question of export. I have not the figure in my mind at the moment ; but it appears to me that a pretty high percentage of our newsprint is exported to the United States. In fact, occasionally you can pick up the comics that are inserted in our Canadian newspapers and find that they have been printed in the United States on newsprint made in Canada. Yet the situation to which I have referred obtains in this country. I know of the letter

which Mr. Bengough wrote in connection with this matter and in which he sets out these facts and offers suggestions. I feel that the matter should be pursued by the government with as much expedition as possible.
If the hon. member can prove that the newspaper industry is a trust or monopoly, why does he not register a complaint? He has a right as a citizen to do so.

He would not get a
decision.
The inference is that newsprint is a monopoly. Can the hon. member vouch for that statement? If so, why does he not complain to the courts?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: The hon. member has corrected himself. He said previously the newspaper business and now he says newsprint. There is quite a difference. Some of the facts to which I have referred are known, namely, the difficulty that certain newspapers have in getting newsprint; and the document to which I have referred is public property, namely, the claim by the newsprint people that they have had to institute their own control to take the place of the control formerly exercised by the wartime prices and trade board. When the newsprint people admit that they have their own control, and the result of that control is that papers like the Vancouver Sun, which is no C.C.F. paper by any means, cannot get sufficient quantities of paper to meet the demands from its subscribers and also to meet the demand for advertising space, it does suggest that there is something which should be looked into. I have been careful not to make any allegation or charge. I am stating what appears to some people to be pretty close to the line. The combines investigation branch should look into the matter and we should know something about it.

ability and standards of the employees, the officials, the guards and wardens, will the minister give consideration to having these officials made permanent under the Civil Service Act? I should like to get some information from the minister regarding the superannuation of officers in the penitentiaries. The thing that worries me is that when they have paid the debt they owe they will still have to keep on paying until they die. I have here three cases which I have worked out. I have the particulars of each of them and I will give the first one. This officer began service with the penitentiary branch in 1921 at Stony Mountain. He elected to come under the superannuation fund in 1944. He found at that time that he was SI,600 in arrears, plus four per cent interest, which amounted to S800 that he had to pay extra. He could not pay this amount in a lump sum, so that he elected to pay for life $17.02 plus current superannuation until he should retire from the service. After having paid! for twr years, that is, to date, he finds that he still has eleven years to pay before reaching the age of sixty-five. That means he will have to pay S17.02 a month for thirteen years, When he will have paid S2,655.12. He found also that he will have paid more than the original amount, and he still has to pay $17.02 until he dies. At the time he elected to come under the superannuation fund he had served twenty-four years and he stood to gain, through a gratuity of one month's pay for every year he served, or approximately $3,000 which he forfeited by coming under the superannuation fund. He was earning 8125 a month at the time. If he stays in the service until he retires at the age of sixty-five he will have served thirty-seven years. He wall draw a pension of $123.78, less S17.02, which will
Supply-Justice

leave him $106.76. He had been earning S2.004 each year for the last ten years. I could give the other cases too; they are similar to this one. They will have paid everything they owe to the government in connection with the superannuation scheme. The first man, if he retires at the age of sixty-five, will pay SH-O? for the other three years, and at t'he age of sixty-eight he will have paid everything he owed. The other fellow pays $16.42 and he will have paid everything at the age of sixty-eight. Another man pays $23.70 and at the age of sixty-nine he will have paid everything. If these fellows live to the age of eighty they have to keep on paying that money. Can the minister explain why they have to keep on paying that money after they have made good their debt?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I cannot explain it offhand, but I suspect the reason is that, should they have died earlier, they would have paid less than the amount that would be sufficient from the point of view of the fund. Is that not the reason?

I do not think so. I do not know of any other superannuation scheme in connection with the government or any other service where a man, after paying what he is entitled to pay according to the regulations or the fund, has to keep on paj-ing after he is superannuated. I can see the force of one man paying for three years, another for three and another for four, because they were later coming in and had to make up the difference. These fellows paid four per cent compound interest on the arrears of the debt, but when they have paid that they will still have to pay from $17 to $20 a month until the day they die. I am not going to hold up the item any longer if the minister will assure me that he will look into the question. I have these cases typewritten so that there will not be any mistake about the matter, and I can give them to the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: This is not a separate scheme. It is not like the R.C.M.P. pension scheme we were discussing earlier in the evening, a thing by itself. This is a well known superannuation scheme covering all civil servants, the same as exists everywhere, and it is a generous and just scheme. I feel sure that there must be some explanation and a good explanation of the facts.
That is what I am trying to find out.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The hon. member has sprung it upon me rather suddenly.

I shall be only too pleased to give the minister time to look into it. He need not give me an answer tonight, so long as he does give me an answer, in order that I may go back to these men and tell them why they have to keep on paying to the end of the chapter.

The answer is this, is it not, that it is part of the scheme, and if these men were not to pay after superannuation they and others would have to pay before superannuation? I think it is just part of a scheme which is not unknown in other walks and callings.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I think so. The hon. gentleman wants some explanation for his correspondents and I will get it from the finance department, who have charge of the superannuation scheme. I desire to draw the minister's attention to what he said in the house on June 3. As reported at page 3740 of Hansard, he said:
. . . There will be occasions later in the session when these matters can be discussed more properly than they can be on this bill.
I understood at that time that the minister proposed to make a statement beyond anything he has so far made in the house as to his approach to this question. Am I right in thinking that the minister is not proposing to make any statement now?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Naturally I have given some thought to whether or not I should make a statement and to just how far I should go. I think I have gone quite a distance already this session. In the first place, we secured this report from General Gibson, and I tabled the report. I said that the government was in accord with the recommendations of that report, at least generally speaking, and would proceed with the carrying out of those recommendations. That was a first step and, in my judgment, a wise and practical step with regard to the penitentiary system. I do not know that I should be expected to go very much farther. That report has a great deal in it. I said that there are some things which I am not in favour of, not in that report, but in certain other reports. I think I have gone about as far as I should go in placing myself or the government on record at this stage.
I listened to the hon. gentleman's speech asking us to proceed and saying there should be a greater note of urgency in what we say about this penitentiary question. I have taken that all to heart; I understand exactly what.

he means. There has been an immense amount of discussion over the years about our methods. I do not know that it is so, that we are so far behind the rest of the world; and when I hear about a lot of these modern methods I am not sure exactly what is meant. I find that great confusion and great differences of opinion exist as to just what methods should be applied. I have read the Saskatchewan report, which is interesting, but I am not prepared to stand here and make a pronouncement upon penological principles or a statement about the relative advantages of the penological approach and the psychiatric approach, about which there seems to be quite a lot of discussion. We shall set up our commission just as soon as we can, and proceed just as quickly as we can.

I am not going to take time to labour this point. I think I fully understand the difficulties the minister has outlined, and I believe I fully understand his unwillingness to step out and make a statement ex cathedra about a lot of things until he has had a chance to consider them. But I would make this point, that I believe the people of this country are entitled-obviously not tonight, and I am afraid not this session, but as soon as possible -to much more from the minister than we have ever had. I believe the people of Canada, particularly those who are concerned about this matter, of whom there are many, are entitled to more than merely a report by a commissioner, though I think that report is very good and I believe the commissioner is a good man. The people are looking for something from the minister as to what he believes about this thing, what his aims and objectives are. He has not had much time to prepare that. I am not going to labour the point further now, but I suggest that before too long-I hope it might be early in the next session of this parliament-we may have from him a considered statement as to what his aims and objectives are and what his approach is to this whole question. Up to the present I submit that it has been a rather mechanical matter; we have dealt with this, that and the other point. Now I think we want to know his approach to this question in a broad and philosophic manner.

Possibly the minister
would not object to saying whether the attitude of his department in appointing one commissioner is to be interpreted as abandoning forever some of the main points of the Archambault report. I have understood that this was a beginning, that it does not neces-

Supply-Justice
sarily mean that the minister or the government is eliminating finally any of the recommendations of the report.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
That is correct. It does
not mean that we are definitely and permanently opposed to those recommendations. I think at the present time the step we are taking is the proper one. I do not believe it is possible at the present time to centralize in the federal authority control of all the prisons in Canada. I do not think it is possible, and I do not think it is desirable. The time may come when it is both, and when that time comes we may have an elaborate organization here at Ottawa; we may have a board and conduct all the parole activities of the country from Ottawa. That may happen, but I am not advocating it at the moment. I agree with the hon. gentleman that when we start in this way it does not mean that we are eliminating the possibility that something else may come in time. It may.
